TAKEN WITH SPRING FEVER. Spring! • To be sure—so it is—and I'm going to sing, Not the tunes that the regular poets rehearse In ridiculous verse. I've nothing of winds aromatic to say, Nor pansies, nor tulips, nor hyacinths gay. I live in the city, And discover no pretty Green leaflet or bud Sticking out of the mud; Nor do I hear warble of blaok bird or blue; Yet I know it is spring just as well as you do. Ay, I know it too well, for its all spring to me, From long before breakfast 14:1 long after tea. I spring with the mats and the rug out-of-doors; I spring to the carpets—drag them from the floors; I spring up step ladders and wash:down the ,walls I spring to the windows, I spring to the halls; I spring to each corner, each closet, each nook; I spring to each dust-laden picture and book; I spring to the garret, where cobwebs abound; I spring (if I may be allowed the expressiod).to .the cellar, half-way underground; I spring—but, good gracious! to tell everything I spring at would take me the whole of the spring, And when spring is over I feel, I declare, _ As though my springs were broken beyond all repair. Spring! To be sure—so it is—but let nobody bring Any poems to me about beautiful flowers, . Or live-giving showers, Or vine-covered bowers, Or sunshiny hours; For really such things seem extremely unmeaning To one on whom spring springs a lot of spring clean- ing.

SOMEWHERE. Somewhere the wind is blowing, I thought as I toiled along In the the burning heat of the noontide, And the fancy made me strong.' Yes, somewhere the wind is blowing, Though here where I gasp and sigh, Not a breath of air is stirring, Not a cloud in the burning sky. Somewhere the thing we long for Exists on earth's wide bound, Somewhere the sun is shining ' When winter nips the ground. • Somewhere the flowers are springing, Somewhere the corn is brown, • And ready unto the haryest • To feed the hungry town. Somewhere the twilight gathers And weary men lay by The burden of the daytime, And wrapped in slumber lie. Somewhere the day is breaking, And gloom and darkness flee; ' Though storms our bark are tossing, / There's somewhere a placid sea. And thus, I thought, 'tis always, • • j• In this mysterious life, • There's always gladness somewhere In spite of its pain and strife; And somewhere the sin and sorrow Of earth are known no more, Somewhere our weary spirits Shall find a peaceful shore. Somewhere the things. that try us

Shall all have pass&l away, - And doubt and fear no longer Impede the perfect day. 0 brother, through the darkness Around thy soul,be cast, The earth is rolling sunward And light shall come at last .—Alfred Capel Shaw in Good Wards for March.

"Time works wonders," said a young man of twenty- seven, when he returned home and found his elder risters • only eighteen. When the Duke of York was obliged to retreat before the French, Sheridan gave as a toast :—" The Duke of York and his brave followers." • Now often has adversity developed strength, energy, fortitude, and persistence that prosperity could never have produced! How often has the dignity of self- support and self-respect been gained when an external prop has been removed! During Sheridan's last illness, the medical attendants, apprehending that they would be obliged to perform an operation on him, asked him "if he had ever undergone I one." "Never." replied Sheridan," except when sitting for my picture, or having my hair cut." The butler of a certain Scottish laird, who had been in 1 the family for many years, at last resigned his situation because his Lordship's wife was always scolding him. ' "Oh I" exclaimed his master, "if that be all, ye've very little to complain of." "Perhaps so," replied the butler; but I have decided in m, own mind to put up with it no longer." "Go, then,' said his Lordship, "and be thankful for the rest of your life that you are not mar- ried to her." Mr. Atkinson, of the States, tells this dramatic story of I his visit to the citadel at Quebec :—" An officer," said he, , "detailed a man to show me around, and he took me everywhere. Noticing a small black cannon, half hiddenl by the snow, as I was about to go, I said in fun: 'I guess I'll :take it away with me." Go look at the in- I acription on the breech,' said the soldier, laughing. I I looked and read: Taken at the battle of Bunker Hill, I June 17, 1775.' I saw the soldier had me. It stirred my blood and I wanted to make a fit reply. I read the in- scription over again to gain time. Tears came to my eyes. 'Young man,' I said to him, you've got the can- non, but we've got Bunker Hill." An old servant named Betsy was with the elder , Herschel at the time of constructing his telescope, and his first act, on discovering the planet Uranus, was to give her a guimia, adding, "You slat Ilthave five guineas, Betsy, when I discover another."l2;The poor woman accepted the offer in all seriousness, and great was her interest in all her master's subsequent labours. Planets, however, even by a Herschel, are not to be discovered I every day, and Betsy's hopes were long deferred. One day Herschel received a friend, to whom he had pre- viously told the Story, with the exclamation, "I have paid my five guineas." " What !" exclaimed the friend; "have we to rejoice over another discovery?" "No, replied the astronomer, with a benevolent smile, "I have simply paid poor Betsy in advance. You see," he added, I as his visitor looked puzzled, "I often pursue these researches long after the poor woman has retired to rest. How is Betsy to know that I do not discover new planets clandestinely, and keep from her the knowledge, with a mean determination to save my money? Better to pay it at once." TKE Yomso Ferinnt.—" There !" said the nurse, I proudly, as she put the new baby into the young father'sl arms, " she's a perfect beauty of a child. —"ls' that all there is of her?" he asked. "I'm ashamed of you." "Wall, this is all clothes, so far as I can see." Then he I took it and turned it head down. "Oh !" screamed the I nurse, "you'll kill the baby !" "Why, what's the mat- I ter?" "Your holding her upside down." "Well, it I doesn't make any difference yet, does it ?" "I never I saw a man so ignorant." "how do you hold her, any- way ?" Then the nurse showed him. "I wonder what a father does under the circumstances," he thought to himself. "1 suppese I've got to talk to the little thing." And he began a string of baby talk. The baby did not show the faintest sign of recognition. "Say, I'm afraid she's deaf, nurse?" "Deaf! You're a fool." "Well, she doesn't hear. She doesn't even— The baby set up a terrible' yell. "She's sick," he said. "There's some- thing the matter with her." "No there aint." "Oh, do babies yell like that so soon?" The baby kept up a bawl. "I don't know about this. I suppose I ought to play the stern parent and spank her, oughtn't I?" "Spank her! I'd like to see you try to spank the dear little thing." "Here, take her away." And he went off down' stairs and lit a cigar and took a walk, reasoning to him- self that there were some things in life only a woman seemed to grasp thoroughly. CATS AND CLOVER.—What connection there is between the prosperity of the pastoral interest and the number of cats in a district might seem difficult to trace; yet tlin relationship is not quite so far-fetched as the words might at first seem to indicate. One of the best-known facts in botany is that many species of plants cannot be fertilised without the agency of insects. The bee or other bisect flying about in search of food, unconsciously carries the pollen of one plant and deposits it On the stigma of another, thus imitating the physiological act without which the seeds on which the plant depends for its reproduction could not be perfected. Among these plants the red clover is one. Unless the humble-bee can reach it, no seeds will be produced, no other species being able to get at the nectar, and—as the agent in the process of fertilisation does not work for the mere good of the piant—at the pollen which it is dastinffl to carry to the nearest clover flower it alights on. Hence, it is highly probable that, if this species of bee became extinct, the red clover would either become very rare or disappear. Now, as the principal enemy of the humble- bees is the field-Mouse, which destroys their combs and nests, but which is itself preyed upon by cats, that the presense of this it is not straining bio-logic to assert, as did Mr. Darwin, quadruped in large numbers determines, through the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of clover flowers in any particular district. Near villages and towns, the nests of humble-bees are more numerous than elsewhere, owing to the number of i cats that destroy the mice. Hence it s fairly deducible from the facts mentioned that the pastoral interests, and inferentially thew of man, are largely dependent, first on bees' then on mice, and, last of all, on cats--possibly, we might add, on single ladies with an affection for these feline pets. We learn wisdom from failure much more than from success. We often discover what will do by finding out what will not do; and probably he who never made a mistake never made a discovery. When you say such and such a man is a "brick," do you think or do you know the origin of it? It is said to be this. An Eastern prince, on being asked, "Where are the fortifications of your city?" replied, pointing to his soldiers, "Every man you see is a brick." Roger relates that, during Hastings' trial, Sheridan, having observed Gibbon among the audience, took occa- sion to mention "the luminous author of 'The Decline and Fall'." After he had finished, one of his friends re- proached him with flattering Gibbon. "Why, what did I say of him ?" asked Sheridan. "You called him the luminous author," &c. " Luminous ! Oh, I meant— voluminous." The labourer who Wears out all his powers in the machinery of life's work, and takes no part in its thought and imagination, and the thinker who wears out his brain before its time, and has no part in the practical activity of life, have each lost much of the pleasure that rightly belongs to them. They may not be conscious of it, but it is none the less true that the health, happiness, and real effectiveness of every man can be gained only by the harmonious union of labour and thought. At the best, no one can know much. Compared with the infinite realms above and beyond us to be yet dis- covered, the knowledge of the most learned man covers but a tiny spot; and what fraction of such a spot ours • may cover is but a small matter. But it does matter to ourselves, and to all around us, the use we shall make of • what we possess—whether we shall carry it around for exhibition, or whether we shall convert it into a living force to elevate our own natures and to bless and help mankind. It is related of a successful Glasgow merchant that, sight-seeing in Paris once, he lost his way. For a con- siderable time he wandered about trying to find his way back. It got late. He could speak no French, and his Glasgow English only brought a smile and a shake of the head. "0 for a body wi' a gnid Scotch tongue in their head." Then came a happy thought. By signs he bought the basket, measure, and berries of a trim French woman, and shouldering the stock-in-trade went along the street yelling, "Fine grossetts, a bawbee the pint; fine gros- setts, a bawbee the pint." The crowd laughed at the mad Briton, but the familiar cry soon brought some Scotsmen on the scene, and the merchant was able to retire from business and smoke his pipe in the bosom of his family, thankful that he had found heal Scotsmen in his hour of need. When Dr. Chalmers became minister of IClmany, in the north of Fife, he used to get his supplies from Anstru- then On one occasion—so the story runs—he sent a written order for a sack of corn to a Mr. Thomson there. The corn never came, and Mr. Chalmers was much annoyed. Next time he was in Anstruther he called on Mr. Thomson for an explanation. It was soon given. The merchant had been unable to decipher the minister's hieroglyphics and had put the note in his desk until Mr. Chalmers should call. "Not make out my writing!" ex- claimed Mr. Claalmbers, indignantly, "show it to me." , He read a few words, but then he stuck, completely baffled. He was, however, equal to the occasion. With a pawky smile he returned the letter to the merchant, , saying, But the letter is addressed to you, Mr. Thom- !ion ; it is your business to read it, not mine." ARMOUR AT TIER CONQUEST.—The principal garment worn in battle at this time by both Normans and Eng- lishmen who were rich or powerful (for the ordinary people fought in their everyday clothes) was so shaped 1 as to cover the arms to the elbow and the legs to the I knee It was made of leather or strong cloth, on which I • were sewed small plates or rings of metal. It was pro- bably also wadded, as an additional protection. Some- ' ernes, instead of the plates or rings, a trellikwork of leather was made and strengthened with seeds. The garment had a square opening in the breast, to enable the 1 wearer to struggle into it, first his legs, then one arm, then the other. When he was in, a flap was buckled or buttoned across the opening. A hood of the same mate- rial as this body garment covered the head and shoulders. On the top of the hood was placed a helmet of iron and bronze, conical or nearly so in shape, and fitting round the head like a hat. A piece of iron came down from the rim in front, protecting the nose and partially masking the face. There was sometimes a similar piece to cover the back of the head and the nape of the neck. These helmets must have been both heavy and uncomfortable, as the whole weight rested on the head, and a perfect fit must have been difficult to obtain. William and one or two of his greatest nobles wore hose protected by plates or rings, like their coats; but most men, noble and simple, relied in battle on an elaborate arrangement of straps reaching from the knee to the ankle and recalling that worn to-day by the peasants of the ankle, Campagna. On their left arms the warriors carried almond-shaped shields, three or four feet long. , For these the English sometimes substituted round or oval shields. The shield was probably made of wood, , covered with leather, and having a border of metal and a projection, or boss, of metal in the widest part. The studs which held the straps by which the shield was I carried also appeared on the outside. The surface, 1 slightly curved and generally of one plain colour with a border, was sometimes decorated with colour lines, a cross, or the figure of a dragon.—Scribner's Magazine. Holm Enocanotr.—Mothers, and all, indeed, interested in the training of the young, would do well to read I earnestly the eight lectures on "Home Education" de- livered last winter in Bradford by Charlotte M. Mason I (published by Kegan Paul and Co.). They dwell on many important subjects which religious parents are in danger of neglecting while diligently attending to the spiritual interests of their children. If none of the func- tions of mind are performed without real activity in the mass of gray and white nervous matter called the brain, the important question arises, What are the conditions of healthy brain-activity? The answer is given under the headings—Exercise, Rest and Change of Occupation, Nourishment, Pure Air, Sunshine, and Free Perspiration. Though the brain of a man weighs only a fortieth part of the body, yet a fifth ;or a sixth of his blood is re- quired for its nourishment. But the body of the child, and in particular the brain, are proportionately more active than the man's, and the child has in addition to grow. Hence the necessity of children being well fed. To secure good air they should be accustomed, we are told, to sleep with at least an inch of open window all through the year, and with much more in summer; and it should be remembered that in ordinary circumstances night air is more wholesome than day air. Whether what is said on the physiology of habit be found correct or not, there can be no doubt about the strange power for good or evil possessed by habits, and the importance, therefore, of labouring to form those that are good. In physical activity the newly-growing muscles themselves take form according to the action required of them. Certain habits of body grow thus into a person and become part of himself, the muscles conforming themselves and growing to the different kinds of action. The author argues that habits not in any sense physical, such as flippancy, truthfulness, order, also make their mark upon a physical tissue, and that it is to this physical effect the enormous strength of habit is probably due. Nor does it seem surprising that the 1 brain should be modified by the work it has to do. "It I is as if every familiar train of thought made a rut in the nervous system of the brain into which the thoughts run lightly of their own accord, and out of which they can only be got by a great effort of will." Many mental and moral habits are explained, and directions given for their formation. The chapter on bow to secure a vigorous well-disciplined will and a well-instructed conscience merits careful reading. The divine life in the child is next discussed. Among the other subjects found through- out the work are out-of-door life, lessons as instruments of education, the relations between school life and home if e, and "the training of the young maidens at home."

The Duke of Buccleuch has for the third time allowed his Sanquhar and Kirkconnel tenantry a reduction of 15 per cent. Advices from New Zealand by the latest mail indicate ' an unfavourable change in crop prospects owing to excessive heat and drought. I FARMING LOSSRs—The Spectator estimates that the 'squires have lost 30 per cent, of their income in the last ten years, the farmers 60 per cent., and the labourers 10 per cent. The clergy stand in a different position to any of them, and must rank next the farmer in the extent of their loss. We regret to announce the death of Mr. Philip Turner, of the Leen, the well-known breeder of Hereford cattle, who passed away on February 25th, in his 74th year. Mr. Turner had of late years been in somewhat failing health, and his son, Mr. A. P. Turner, had for all practical purposes taken over the management of his affairs. UN PRODUCTITE WHEAT GROWING.—The agricultural editor of the Field mentions the case of a field which had been in bare fallow the previous year, and was under wheat last year, producing grain which only aver- aged £2 15s. 7d. per acre; whereas the cost, excluding the value of manure, would have been at least £5 10s. an acre. The field was well rnanured, but badly drained. TRH GERMINATING QUALITIES OF SRED.—SODIS experi- ments carried out at the Ontario Agricultural College to test the germanating qualities of seed of various kinds ten years old, have given the following percentage of germination:—Tares, 90; mangolds, 72; turnips, 32; buckwheat, 16; clover, 6; timothy grass, 2; barley, oats, rye, beans, and peas, O. Several samples of most varie- ties were tried. In the case of beans, though ten samples failed to germinate, two tried separately gave a percent- age of 36. fIaR9VOLUTION7IN BUTTER' MAgrxe.—An agricultural correspondent of great experience in this district writes:: A new system has been discovered by a Frenchman, which is yet a secret, put if it is as he professes it be, it will be superior to any yet brought before the public. He turns off 1 lb. pure Butter from three gallons of milk. 6 There is no buttermilk; only water, showing that all the substance is absorbed into the butter, which seems to

account for the quantity got. How he gets such a result is a secret, but spectators say it is by the addition of some Chemical substance. The analysts say it is good and pure butter, which those who have tasted will testify. .

EtcTs Aziern. MILK, Cnsam, AND Burreri.—Mr. Robert- son, superintendent of dairying for the province of Ontario, and in charge of the experimental creamery at the Ontario Agricultural College, gives the following as facts, which he says are known to few but experts in the daily business :-1. The natural flavours of milk and its products reside mainly in their fat constituents. 2. While milk is quite new its cream or fatty portion is comparatively insipid or lacking in flavour. 3. By ex- posure to the action of the air (oxidation) the flavour is ripened or developed, and the colour of the cream and the butter made therefrom is deepened. 4. A warm temperature facilitates and a cool temperature re- tards the development of • flavour. 5. That butter made from cream, raised at the ordinary tem- perature of the atmosphere, in open, shallow vessels (such as are commonly used in Brittany, Eng- land, and Ireland), has a fuller and riper flavour, when just made, than butter manufactured from cream raised in deep cans, submerged in cold water, as by the Canadian creamery system. 6. The former butter has its best flavour within two days after it is made, while the latter—the creamerv—may continue to have its best taste fgrm three to Ave weeks afterwards. 7. The earlier development of flavour in that butter which is at its best just after churning proclaims it of tlle character defined by the fruit adage, "Quick ripe, quick rotten." For such butter, delicious while fresh, nobody claims keeping properties any more than for har- vest apples the quality of keeping sound till spring time. 8. On the other hand, the quality of creamery butter (as evidenced by the Ontario Government's dis- play at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition, free for inspection and examination by all interested shows that it has excellent keeping properties. 9. The butter fat of. milk is in the condition of minute globules. These are collected into a mass by the impaction of churning. 10. Any after-working, "muting," or "milling" that destroys the natural grain or texture of butter thereby destroys its keeping properties, just as the bruising of fruit or the breaking of egg-shells renders both of these commodities subject to speedy decay. 11. As an article of diet, delicious butter is very different in its gastro- nomic effect from oleomargarine or any imitation com- pound. 12. Fine butter (its peculiarity) aids weak digestion by instilling its own atoms between the atoms of more solid foods, thus assisting in their disintegration for assimilation.—Breeders' Journal.

How GOOD COWS ARE RUINED.—An experienced writer on the care of animals gives the following advice to far- mers on the subject of milking cows:—" Milking is an art, and the farm hand who knows how to milk properly is more valuable to the careful dairyman than any ether help Of course, anybody can milk, and some can milk a dozen cows before breakfast; the careful manager, however' is not so anxious for fast help as he is to employ those who are careful. The operation should never be hurried, but the milk should be drawn steadily and as it flows, naturally. Some cows have very tender teats, and the rapid milkman forgets this fact in his en- deavour to make speed. The cow that is naturally impatient and fretful does not like to submit to rough handling, and her disposition is soon ruined by such treatment. With the constant irritation she fails in quanity, and is less productive, just as any human being would fail to perform faithful services when labouring under mental affliction or trouble. As the udder be- comes distended and filled with milk, the desire on the part of the cow is to be relieved of its contents, and she willingly submits to it for the relief it occasions. The constant practice of being milked at stated intervals im- presses itself strongly upon her, and she will seldom offer resistance without cause. When a cow, therefore, that has been a patient deliverer of milk becomes fractious, the fault can always be traced to the milkman. The care- less dairyman is the one who complains of the failure ! of his cows to keep up the flow, and bloody milk, gar. get, and other evils are the results of his own bad management. There is another point in the treat- ment of cows that demands attention, and that is allowing them to stand a long time waiting to be , milked. With cows that give large yield it is painful, and when the udders have been filled to their utmost, and the milkman is not on hand to re- __ .

lieve them, they become exceedingly nervous and restless. Tis will do more to cause a cow to go dry before her period than anything else, and many a good Cow has been sent to the shambles through diminution of quantity, simply because nature had revolted at her sufferings, and allowed her to dry up because her store- house was not emptied of its contents at the proper time. She should also be milked to the last drop if possible; and, as the 'last portion of milk is claimed to be the richest, the udder should be left with nothing in it. With regularity in feeding and milking, and kind treat- ment at all times, the cow will not only become gentle, and remain so, but will milk on several weeks longer than otherwise. An experienced dairyman needs help that is skilful, and he knows how to judge the milkman's work by the behaviour of his cows. When a stable of cows begin to give trouble in milking, it is only necessary to observe the manner in which they are milked in order to cure the evil. The udder of a cow is a very delicate structure, and she quickly rebels at rough usage or im- proper periods of milking." HDrrs ON Pm BIIEEDING.—In breeding pigs, the first thing is the selection of the boar to be used in the herd. This is a very important matter, for it has been well said that "the sire is half the herd." In all cases where good results are desired the male must be a pure-bred, of whichever breed that may be deemed best; and here we cannot afford to be niggardly, but should be willing to pay some breeder of repute a good price for a good pig. Assuming that a good male has been selected, two extremes should be avoided in his future care and management. One extreme is to confine him in a close
pen v';here no exercise can be had; the other T's

io turn him out with the entire herd until he be- comes the worst looking pig on the plaee, and then the breed that he represents, as well as the breeder, is blamed ifdr. the bad results that follow. The right. way la-to keep the boar by himse/f when prac- ticable, but exercise must be had. It would be better nut to, use thei boar until nearly or quite one year old, and not exceisively until about two years old. In selecting sows avoid those with coarse heads as much as possible, as a large, coarse head does not indicate a pro- fitable feeder. The best results are generally from matured sire and dams. Possibly the reason for con- stantly using young sows is the belief that it costs more to winter the old sows than the younger ones. This is certainly a mistake, as sows that have attained their growth can be kept at less expense than those that are growing. Perhaps, too, the breeder thinks that the older and larger sows will bring more money on account of their extra weight, and so keeps the younger ones to breed from. Sows can be profitable until they are from four to six years old, if they show themselves to be good, careful mothers. As a rule. the best results come from pigs born in March. The pen that the sow is to farrow in should be warm and dry, at least 7ft. by 7ft. in size, and provided with 6in boards or rails around the sides of the pen, about Bin. from the floor, so that the little fel- lows can find a safe retreat, and avoid being crushed by a clumsy sow when in the act of lying down. Little straw should be furnished her at first, and that must be fine, otherwise the pigs get tangled in the long straw. Sepa- rate the sow from the rest of the herd from one or two weeks before she is to farrow, and see that the system is made free from fever by cooling, laxative food, as oats, bran, shorts, and roots. In fact, this kind of food should be given the sow for some Weeks previous to pigging. For 24 hciurs after farrowing stie should have nothing to eat, but all the water that she needs. If the water is cold the chill should be removed by the addition of sufficient warm water. The sow should be fed very sparingly till, the pigs are at least a week old, and then, as circumstances may seem to warrant, the feed may 134: increased in quantity and quality. Diarrhea in young pigs is usually caused by the fact that the sow has been overfed, in which case the sow should be fed very lightly for a day& two. Farmers who wish to improve their stock of pigs should now be looking up their breeding stock. If already supplied with good brood sows, they

• LONDOI.7. THURSDAY.

The proceedings in the House of Commons this week have dealt yet another blow to the tottering Government. The all-night sitting which carried the House well into Tuesday. after- noon was a lamentable occurrence not calcu- lated to add to the dignity or the use- fulness of Parliament. But it was clearly and directly traceable to astounding mismanagement. All the Government had to do when the House met on Monday was to obtain a particular vote in the Civil Service Estimates. Time had been run so short that it was imperative to pass this vote be- fore the House rose. In such circumstances the least gifted business man might have been expec- ted to bring forward the vote at the earliest. pos- sible moment. Instead of that Lord George Hamil- ton was permitted to bring on at five o'clock the Admiralty Vote, about which there was no particu- lar hurry. This opened the sluices of oratory on the part of the admirals and captains, who talked to each other in an otherwise empty house till mid- night. Then, and apparently only then, it dawned upon Mr. Smith that they were getting into a hole. Steps were hurriedly taken to redeem the fatal error. Lord George got up and announced to the amazed House that he would withdraw the Navy Vote so that they might proceed with the Civil Service Estimates. _ .

This confession of amazing bungling was the Irish members' opportunity. After all the freshest hours of the night had been purposely wasted, here were the Government proposing in the early morning to pass a vote of over three millions sterling! The ground was too tempting not to be occupied by the able and habile party, and member after member rose to protest against the proposal. Then came a fresh and final blunder. It was evident to the least- trained experience that the Irish members, joined by Mr. Labouchere and one or two other Radicals, meant mischief. But within the past two days the Government, with the assistance of the Leaders of the Opposition, had obtained a weapon of defence which, wielded with ordinary skill, would make ohstruction impotent. The Parnellites might, if they liked, obstruct for an hour more or less. Then the Cloture would be moved, and business would advance. The Parnellites knew this, and sung rather small up to two o'clock in the morning. Then they began to see how the land lay, and forthwith re- solved to carry to the furthest extent the advantage surprisingly left to them. The Government, masters of a well disciplined phalanx had actually failed to keep in hand suffi- cient members to carry on the closure. With a minority of over forty it was necessary that the majority should number at least two hundred. It was evident from the hurried movement of the Whips, and the consternation that began to show itself on the Treasury Bench, that this number was not available. The Treasury messengers were out all over the West End, knocking up members and almost carrying them off by force to recruit Minis- terial ranks. At three o'clock in the morning the unwonted apparition of Mr. Christopher Sykes in curiously rough-and-tumble attire, cheered the hearts of the Ministerialidts. Then a division was tried, and to the chagrin of Ministers and to the uncontrollable delight of the Parnellites, it was found that there were only 199 Conservatives, one less than the number requisite to carry the closure. Fresh relays of messengers were sent out, the doors were vigilantly guarded, so that no sleepy and pairing Conservative might escape. In single num- bers and at long intervals recruits dropped in, and when the night was far advanced the closure was carried, but only with seven men to spare. This total absence of managerial ability has, in political circles, shaken the Government even more than would have been done by a more serious ad- ministrative mistake. Their position is, indeed, in other respects pitiful. It is whispered that the health of Lord Salisbury is in a much more serious condition than is publicly admitted. If he were compelled to follow Sir M.ll Beach into retirement what would become of the Conservative party? Who is there to succeed Lord Salisbury? Only Lord Randolph Churchill, who is hovering about and promises to be back presently. Lord Randolph's accession to power would, of course, mean a thorough reconstruction of the Ministry, and the adoption of a Home Rule scheme, at least as thorough as Mr. Gladstone's. Meanwhile the sheet anchor of the storm-driven and belated Government is the adherence of the Dissentient Liberals. It is understood that with two exceptions (which do not include Mr. Chamberlain) these gentlemen will carry out their absorbing desire to block Mr. Glad- stone's return to power even to the extent of voting for the Coercion Bill. But this unnatural alliance can be but temporary, and, to those Liberals who think chiefly of tactical advantage, is not unwel- come. It serves a double purpose. It will ruin the political chances of all quondam Liberals who take part in the confederacy, and it will stave off for this session the resignation of the Government, a con- summation which, as I have shown before, is de- voutly wished for. , Lancashire has within the past week provided the House of Commons with two surprises, one of a most painful character. No one in political circles was thinking of Mr. J. K. Cross when neivs came of his melancholy death. At one time he filled a considerable space in the Parliamentary horizon. He seemed marked out for high office, and would doubtless have obtained it if he had chanced to be in the House when M. Gladstone was called upon to form a fresh administration after the General Election last year. But, suffering in the havoc that befel many Liberals at that election, he dropped entirely out of sight iiflcl nut of mind. People who knew him casually, hear with surprise that he was a great sufferer. Ile generally looked the perfection of health, bright-eyed, and. ruddy. I remember Lulu years ago meeting him in the House after a brief Easter holiday, and noticing his apparently , boisterous health, I made some remark about it. Ah," he said, in a tone of deep melancholy that greatly struck me, "I may look well, but I'm not." He suffered from a pecular and rare disease which inflicted intolerable pain during its paroxysms. At a later period, when he had been for a few months Under Secretary of State for India, he told me that he felt he would have to give up the work, which, in his state of health, was more than he could stand.

The other event alluded to is the marriage of Mr. T. B. Potter. Since his first wife's death; which took place a little more than a year ago, Mr. Potter, once the most constant attendant upon the business of the House, has been very rarely seen there. But no one suspected what was occupying the young fellow's thoughts during these past months. Feed him with apples, for he is apparently sick of poli- tics, and the House of Commons will know him no more as it was wont. The:place is, indeed, very much altered from what it was when, nearly a qua/ter of a century ago, Mr. Potter first took his seat as member for Rochdale. Even up to the time Parliament dissolved in 18.35, Mr. Potter enjoyed his corner seat below the gangway unchallenged. But nothing is sacred to the Parnellite, and if Mt. Pot- ter were to come in any evening now he would find his seat appropriated. So he wisely stops away. and has found content in other paths than the poli- tical one.

1 The impression that trade has this time really started on the high road of improvement is every- where prevalent. I have not noticed any reference to the state of affairs in the market for chemicals, which, it will be remembered, Mr. Disraeli once

THE LATE LORD GERARD. FUNERAL AT ASHTON.

The interment of the remains of the late Lord Gerard, of Brynn, took place in the church-yard of St. Oswald's Catholic Church, Liverpool-road, Ash- ton-in-Makerfield, on Saturday at noon. • The an- nouncement of the death of Lord Gerard, under the sudden circumstances reported in our last issue, threw a gloom over the district of which he was so prominent a resident, and with which a long line of ancestors of the Gerard family had been so intima- tely associated. Though comparatively few details of the sad event were publicly known, the death of the de- ceased baron formed almost the one mournful topic of conversation throughout, the neighbourhood. It has been ascertained that his lordship retired to rest at his London residence, 16, South-street, Park. lane, at his usual hour on Monday evening week, being then attended by his valet. Next morning the valet took a cup of tea into the bedroom, but, as .his lordship appeared to be asleep, he left the cup of tea in the bedroom and withdrew. Going into the room again to light the fire he found the tea untouched, and, to arouse Lord Gerard, he made a noise with the fire-irons. This had no effect, and the valet on closer examination found his master dead. The body showed no indication of the deceased hav- ing struggled or suffered pain, and the countenance was tranquil as if in ordinary sleep. The sad news was at once telegraphed to Garswood and to the Rev. Father O'Reilly at Ashton, at both of which places the intelligence occasioned profound regret. The body of the deceased, after having been en- closed in the coffin, was conveyed by the night ex- press for the north, leaving London at ten o'clock on Thursday night, and arriving at Newton- bridge Station about four o'clock on Friday morn- ing. From here the body was conveyed in a hearse to St. Oswald's Church, where it was placed on a bier in front of the altar. It remained there until the time of interment. The interior of the sacred edifice, including the altar, bier, reserved pews, gas standards and .brackets, pulpit, walls, &c., were draped with purple cloth, and there were other evidences of a desire to show the keen sorrow felt at the loss sustained by one of the noblest suppor- ters of the handsome country church. The old burial place of the Gerard family was at Winwick Church, while many years ago there was an inter- ment at the old Windleshaw Abbey ground, near St. Helens, but at the wish of the deceased lord, a new family vault has been commenced on the west side of St. Oswald's Church, and the coffin containing his remains has been the first to be placed therein. The family arrangements for the funeral were of a quiet and unostentatious nature, but the religious portion of the mournful proceedings was eminent- ly appropriate as a last opportunity of paying per- sonal tribute to the memory of the deceased lord. The members of the family, and the more intimate friends visiting at Garswood Hall, were conveyed in carriages to the Church, where they occupied re- served seats in the centre, while the gentry of the district occupied the remainder of the building. Of the general public there was a very large attend- ance, many of whom were unable to gain admission. The Dowager Lady Gerard was unable to attend the services owing to the severe illness occasioned by the shock at the receipt of the sad news of her husband's death. The principal mourners were the Hon. William Causeffeld Gerard (eldest son of the late peer, who succeeds to the title and estates), the present Lady Gerard, Hon. Robert Gerard (younger son), Hon Mrs. Oliphant (daughter) and Colonel Oliphant, Hon. Mrs. :Gosselin (daughter) and Mr. Gosselin, Captain Edward Gerard (nephew), Sir John Lawson, Mr. Milner, and Mr. Gerard May- nail (London, solicitor to the late peer). Among the large number of gentlemen who attended were the Hon. and Rev. Canon Bridgeman (rector of Wigan), Rev. H. Siddall (Ashton), Rev. W. J. Mel- ville (rector of Downall Green), Lieut.-Colonel F. W. Earle, J.P., Lieut.-Colonel Richard Pilkington, J.P. (Rainford Hall), Captain A. R. Gladstone, J.P., Major Ralpha, Captain and Adjutant More- land, Captain Withington, J.P. (Lowton), Mr. J. Gaskell, J.P. (Ashton), Mr. H. S. Hall, J.P. (St. Helens), Mr. A. Park, J.P. (Mayor of Wigan), Dr. A. Handyside (Earlestown), Messrs C. F. Clarke, R. A. Ffarington, T. D. Grirake (Golborne), W. Valiant, (Ashton), J. S. Eccles and Robinson (St. Helens), T. Pearson, M. Brown-Westhead, B. B. Glover, J. E. Pardey, and R. H. Wright (Newton), W. Balharry (Ilaydock), Robins (steward to the late peer), P. Ball (clerk of works), McGill (surveyor), and Fer- guson (farm bailiff). The service in church commenced about eleven o'clock, and was conducted by the Right Rev. Dr. O'Reilly, the Catholic Bishop of Liverpool. The pulpit still remained on the bier fronting the altar, but it was almost hid from sight amid an immense number of magnificent wreaths. The service, in- cluding the requiem mass, was of an imposing and impressive character. The Bishop was assisted by the Very Rev. Canon Carr (Liverpool), vicar general; the Rev. Father D. Sommer (Wigan), and Austin Powell (Birchley), deacons of the throne ; Rev. Father John Chapman, deacon of the mass; Rev. Fekther T. Myerscough, sub-deacon of the mass; and the Rev. Father C. Green, bishop's secretary; and T. Spencer (Ainsdale), master of ceremonies. The music was Gregorian, and was rendered by a choir comprising the following priests : Rev. Fathers A. Bennelt (Waterloo), T. Hawksworth (Chorley), R. Bridges (St. Joseph's College, Uphol- land), John Melling (Wigan), J. McFarlane (Wigan), and W. Byrne (Golborne). The other clergy pre- sent were Fathers John Lennon (Wild Bank), J. Lennon (Newton), Richard O'Neil (Tyldesley), M. Doon (Orrell) J. Waring (Pemberton), R. Barry (Standish), J. Hanley (Ince), Thomas Margison (Wrightington), T. Gradwell (Wigan), Cardwell (St. Helens), Dignam (St. Helens), Egger (St. Helens), Ullathorne (St. Helens), O'Sullivan (Black- brook), and W. Walmesley (St. Helens). At the close of the service the Very Rev. Canon Carr, Vicar General, gave an address upon the words—" The keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall stagger, and they shall shut the door upon the street, and they shall fear high things, because man shall go into the house of his eternity. The silver cord shall be broken, and the golden fillet shrink back, and the pitcher be crushed at the fountain, and the wheel be broken at the cistern, and the dust return unto the earth from whence it was, and the spirit return to the God who gave it. Vanity of vanities, all things are vanity. (Ecclesiastes xii chap.) The coffin was then borne to the vault In the churchyard the choir of priests chanting an appropriate dirge along the path. The vicinity of the grave was roped off tá prevent a crash by the general public, while a number of police offi- cers, under :the charge elf Superintendent Heywood, were also present. The coffin was of polished oak, with brass fittings, and an ornamental crucifix, and upon a plate was the inscription—" Robert Telver, first Baron Gerard, born May 12th, 1808, died March 15th, 1887." The service at the graveside was concluded by the Bishop of Liverpool, and after the relatives and mourners had moved away the public were admitted to view the coffin, vault, and the wreaths. Among the contributors of wreaths and crosses were Mr. Henry Petra, Mrs Ince Anderton, Miss Keiffm- hein, Miss Maud Anderton, Ashton Conservative Club, Catholic School children, La Marquesa de Santurce, Mrs Emily H. Pfachler, Miss Pfachler, Rev. Canon Bennett, Mr. T. W. Legh., M.P., and Mrs Legh. the clergy of St. Oswald's, Ashton tenants, Windle and Billinge tenantry, Mr. and Mrs Brown•Westhead, Lord Gerard's household, , Mr. Hector Toler, Major C. H. SERIOUS OUTBREA:C. OF .ANTHRgiCi

IN CHESHIRE. ' • A meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held at the Town Hall, Chester, on Saturday, tinder thripresideocy of the Mayor of Chester, to listen tca:ti paper on milk, by Mr. C Jorge Willis, manager of the Cheshire Deiry Institute. There was a very large Yst- teridance, and after the reading of the paper, Mr- Thomas Itigby,secretary of the chamber, rose and said herhad one matter to bring before the chamber of a veryamd nature. Most of them had experience -or he cattle plaguet 20 years ago, and a terrible expe. .e.312T had also had pleuro-pneumonia and fi ,i 4. disease. Lot now there was a disease breaking-out:hi one part of the county which was almost as:. rapidly fatal as the cattle plague. It was called! anthrax, and was attacking cattle and pigs especially:l and cheep and lamba. No one had yet been able,toi point out the cause of this disease. There was no sort, of remedy for it known, and it was very quickly fatal. If .it continued to go on HA it threatened to do, they ivould need to press it upon the attention of theGovernr', mentand on the attention of the county authority. Mr. Henry Linaker, of Frodsharn, who came from the dis- trict in which the disease had broken out, gave the Chamber some information cefueerning it. The disease. broke out on Friday week on a farm in the townahip Aston, on which there was a large herd of dairy and tat' cattle, a large flock of sheep, and a very large number of pigs. Since that time there had died or been slaugh- tered upwards of 30 pigs, and several cows and sheep, and this was going on up to that.time. The diseaseamas sudden and fatal. In five or six hours after the animal. was attacked it was dead. There was no time to call ix the inspector in many cases. There was no time to. order the slaughter of the animal so that ft' was becoming a very serious matter indeed.. It was called splenier, apoplexy, and was tiaift to affect individuals as well as animals. It was said not to be contagious, but it was a strange fact that in the case in question the disease brolre out in dlf-i fereat parts of the farm. He had that morning reoehredi Information that the county authority had Mimed notice proscribing the movement of cattle in the district affected.—At a meeting of the Council of the Chamber. of Agricniture held subsequently, the secretary now Instructed to write to the Privy Council, giving the-facto which had been named referring to this disease, and ha' ask that a veterinary inspector or botanist, or both, if .deemed desirable, might be sent down to inspect and. give.their opinion as to the steps to be taken; also that the Privy Council should be memorialised to place the, disease on the same list as pleuro-pneumonia and foot-y and-mouth disease, as far as controlling movements compensation when slaughter is determined upon.-1t was arranged to report to the next meeting a thei Council.

The farm in question has been held, I believe, by the. present occupiers upwards of ten years. During that; period and for some years previously many cattle dart other animals which have been located on it have elk& more or less suddenly every year, the deaths =caw the cattle alone ranging from ten to twenty or mote„i and occurring usually between March and the! autumn mor.tbs. A former 'occupier of the fartni is said to lia.to had a large tank into which the camases- of diseased animals were thrown, and occasionally-alb, was emptied and its contents distributed on the land.. Messrs. Percival have not utilised their dead animals Jill the same way, but occasionally and very recently their pigs have obtain( d access to the flesh of a. horse and. several sheep which had died suddenly. These factsl probably afford a due as to the cause of the present out.'i break. On March 11 one of the breeding sows was per-i ceived to be seriously ill, and on being examined after death by a reighbouring practitioner her disease wreg, said to he inflammation of the lungs. On March ten more pigs were attacked, and one died. On March 13 five more were found ill and seven died.;, March 14 eighteen attacked and twenty-four died or were destroyed. In addition to these a sheep was,' attacked and died on Alsrch 12, another on March 13;1 and a third on March 14, making a total of thirty-eve; deaths within about sixty hours. On March 18 twol more sows were attacked, and some young ones appeared! to be ailing. No cattle have been attacked during this outbreak, but from long experience Messrs. Percival are aware that such cases may happen at any time. The disease usually kills the animal affected, whether oow„ sheep, or pig, within a few hours. Frequently onei or more have boon left apparently well and found dead or dying the following morning. IMPERIAL PAIILIAMENT- , -------- HOUSE OF LORDS.-.-MONDAT. ' The Lord Chancellor took his seat at four o'clock. i ELECTRIC LIGHTING.—Their Lordships then went into committee en the Electric Lighting Act (18821 Amendment Bill.—On clause 1 the Earl of CAMPERDOWN moved to omit the words bearing upon the sale and purchase of the goodwill of the business of the undertaking."—Lord Twin- Low opposed the amendment, balding that the end both he and the noble Earl were striving for—namely, the creation of a new industry and the prevention of monopoly—would be best attained by adhering to the welds of the clause as they stood.—Their Lordships divided, after some discus- sion, with the following result :—For the amendment 10. against 45. majority against 35. The amendment was therefore lost.—The bill then passed through committee. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. ; The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS, &c.—Sir JAMES FERRUSSON said he hoped to lay on the table before Easter a despatch from the United I States Government on the subject of the Anglo-American fisheries dispute.—Answering Sir H. Tyler, Lord GEORGE HAMILTON said new regulations were being prepared to pre- vent irregularities at the Royal dockyards of the kind re- cently brought to light. His Lordship, in reply to other questions, gave some details of the Jubilee naval review' at which the Queen is to be present, in July, and of the elabo- rate manosuvres which are to be carried out for the purpose of testing our means of coast defence.—Mr. W. H. Storm informed Sir John Swinburne that inquiries into the recent outbreaks of anthrax were being conducted by the officers of the Agricultural Department. THE COERCION BILL.—Mr. BALvorn gave notice that he would next day ask leave to bring in a bill te make bet- ter provision for the prevention and punishment of crime in Ireland, and Mr. W. H. Smith:announced his intention to move that the several stages of the measure should have precedence of all other business whenever the bill was set down as first order of the day. In the event of the bill be- ing brought in next day or on Wednesday, the second read- ing would, said Mr. Smith, be taken on Monday next.—Mr. JOHN MonLET suid be should meet Mr. Smith's motion with an amendment " declining to set aside the business of the nation in favour of a measure for increasing the strin- gency of the criminal law in Ireland whilst no effectual security has been taken against the abase of the law by the exaction of excessive rent."—Mr. SMITH intimated, in reply to a question, that it was the intention of the Chief Secre- tary to make a statement on the subject of the Irish Land Bill almost immediately. SUPPLY.—AN ALL NIGHT SITTING. After the Ministerial announcements on the subject of legislation for Ireland, the House went into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates.—Mr. SHA.W.LEFEVRE re- plied to some of the strictures of the First Lord of the Ad- miralty on the administration of the navy by Lord North- brook,—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON said his desire had been to make his statement free from party colour,and he believed there was a desire in all parts of the House to secure the efficiency of the navy.—The discussion was continued until midnight, when the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER ex- pressed the ksire of the Government to withdraw the vote under discussion in order that a vote on account might be taken.—This was objected to, and as the Government could not apply the closure without reinforcements, the discus- sion proceeded until half-past four o'clock on Tuesday morning when Mr. W. H. SMITH moved the first motion under the new closure rule—" That the question be now put."—The numbers were 209 for, the 54 against, so that the closure was carried, and the vote of naval victualling and clothing was agreed to at five o'clock.—The vote on account of tue Civil Service, amounting to £3,624,000, fol- lowed, and upon it a wearisome discussion was carried en for eight hours, during which time several divisions were taken and some scenes occurred.—At one o'clock the vote on account was agreed to, and at twenty minutes past one the House adjourned, after a sitting of more than twenty- one hours..

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15. Tax CHURCH PATRONAGE BILL. —On the report of amendments to the Church Patronage Bill, Lord Guns- runsmolaserved that the measure would give the bishops greater power than they had possessed in any time of which we had record, in regard to the sale of livings and to presentations, and the effect would be to destroy the value of that description of property and to bring in a worse set of persons. Be proposed the omission from the second clause of the aubetshion which imposed checks upon the sale of advowsons.— The Earl of &mamma held it was necessary to provide some security against, the free traffic in next presenta- tions.—"rhe amendment was negatived art further discussion—The Bishop of LICHFrEtI), with a view of cutting up the root of scandal, proposed that, the auk, of any right of patronage shook! not be valid within a period of five years from the date at which the right of patronage should previously have been sold, unless on the death of the patron for the time being, or if so, with not, less than 20 acres of land.—Earl BEsoorreace opposed. —The Earl of HARIzOwiIY thought the matter was exactly one of those that should be left to the Commis- sioners—The amendment was negatived.—The Bishop of LONDON proposed a clause making it unlawful for the purchase of any advowson or any right to a presentation to a benefice, afterwards on the next avoidance offer himself to the Bishop for admission or institution.— The clause was added to the bill—Earl COWPER pro- posed, in substitution for clause 14, a now clause em- powering the Bishop on the representation of three parishioners to remove an incumbent on the ground that for three years previous he had been incapacitated by continuing bodily or mental infirmity from the due per- formance of his duty.—The new clause was agreed to, and the report was received. Glebe Lands Bill was read a third time and passed. 11,, report of amendments to the Pharmacy Act Amendment Bill was received. Chronaa Srres.—On the motion for going into com- mittee on the Church Sites (Compulsory Powers Repeat) BM, the Bishop of Limarritro explained that its object was to remove from the statute book an obsolete enactment of TO years ago, which conferred upon the Chindi of England alone the power of acquiring by compulsory purchase sites for churches.—The Earl of KIMBERIMt questioned the expediency ot repealing the enactment in question, lest by so doing they should ap pear to be condemning the principle of allowing land to be taken under any errctrrnsta,nceseomptilsonly for places of worship.—Lord Grawruottes regarded the measure as wholly unnecessary.—The motion for going into committee was negatived, and the bill thrown out. It was now in the hands of the draughtsman, and would be both an amending and a consolidating bill In reply to Mr. B. Coleridge, Mr. W. H. Sscrrn said that the report of Mr. Knife, the dissentient member ot Lord Gowper's Irish Land Commission, had now been laid on thetabie. _ .

Slaughter was not necessary in cases of anthrax, as the animals were often found dead, and as the disease did not spread through contact with in- fected animals slaughter would only benefit the owner, and not the community. PRECEDENCE FOR THE COERCION BILL. OPPOSITION AMENDMENT.

Mr. W. H. Sacra rose amid cheers from the Ministerial benches, and ironical cheers from the Opposition, to meve a resotution giving precedence to the introduction and several stages of the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill. He said the Government were induced to bring forward this measure because of the disorganised state of Ireland, and the necessity imposed upon the Executive of seeing that the law was observed. The Government had came to the conclusion that the men- they were about to introduce was demanded for the purpose of enall3ag order to be mamtamea in me in- terests of the peace and happiness of the' law-abiding portion of the Irish people. The powers asked for were necessary to the maintenance of social order. The right hon. g-entlesnan the member for Newcastle had put on the paper an amendment declining to set aside the busi- ness of the nation in favour of a measure for increasing the stringency of the criminal law in Ireland, while no effectual security had been taken against the abuse of the law by the exacting of exces- sive rents. In answer to this, he had to say, on behalf of the Government, that although therwere prepared to deal, and were-dealing, with the land question they could' not take up that question before they had secured the maintenance of the law. The Government could not present to Parliament any measure that-was not framed in the interests of honesty and justice, and he did not anticipate that the measures they might propose would satisfy the apostolic to the .Land League, but those measures would be such as had the careful con- sideration of the Government; and such as it wat hoped would prove effectual for the object in view.

Mr. .L Molnar!, who was received with loud Opposi- tion cheers, rose to move the amendment just read by the First Lord of the Treaeury. He said that amend- mentdisputed the necessity for urgency, and the priority of the Coercion Bill over other mea.sures for Ireland. He oantxmaed that the Government were going to work in an jarrted order, and would weaken by their present action whatever good there -might be in their subsequent proposals. Lord John Russell, speaking of a former coercion bill, had pointed out that it might be more - effectual if accompanied by some remedial legislation. ,and he had gone into the lobby against that pPoposal, compenywith the senior member for Birmingham. What,asked.the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Morley), was thegraand on which the House was nowasked to pass a coercion bill? What were the Government aiming at? They were not trying to put down rebellion, but were acting against a combination to protect the tenants against exactions which the Government, themselves admitted to be oppressive. (Cheers.) The contention of the Opposition had been that tile serious fall of prices had tended to prevent the tenants from paing their rents, and this was borne out by the report of Earl Cowper's Commission. As to the combinations among tt.. to...ars- the .00IMMIS6011tETS were of minion that

they had been mainly eause4 by the excessive rents de- manded of thetenants. ' Moreover, the report was con- clusive that, but for these combinations, many-of the concessions- would have open made by the land- lords, and others which were declared to have been just and reasonable, would not have been made. The bill before the' House was really •a bill to enable !andlords to -exact exorbitant rents, and exces- sive rents. (Hear, hear.) Sir Redvers Buller, one( of the witnesses before the Commissioners, had said do- body had done anything for the tenant until the League was established—(hear, hear)—and he added that it was, In his opinion, the pressure of high rent that had pro- duced the agitation. The effect of this present bill would 'be to throw the law more than ever on the side of the rich, by removing ail the coercive power Sir R. Buller wished to put on the landlords, and placing it 4n the wretched tenants instead. (Cheers.)

Ur. A. J. 13enrona, who rose amid Ministerial cheers, 'teamed Mr. Morley of having bestowed criticism and invective ort measures which he had not seen' and of 'which he' knew nothing. For his own part he (Mr. Balfour) should reserve his defence of the Government, bill till that bill was before the House. Mr. Gladst me had in 1881 told the House that it was to consider, not only the amount of crime, but its character and that at which it aimed. (Cheers.) That was what the Govern- ment said at the present moment. With regard to what had been said as to the fall in prices, that fall had only amounted to one-sixtb of the whole, and this he argued was not sufficient to be the cause of a social revolution. With regard to evictions in Ireland, there were in the last quarter of last year 522 evictions, of which 324 were cases of non-judicial rents. It was beside the ques- tion to tell the House that there were some bad landlords. This must, of course, be expected while human nature remained what it was. Turning to the land legislation passed by the late Government, the right hon. gentleman characterised it as a humiliating failure, and asserted that the conversion of that party to Home Rule was a confession of that failure. In conclusion the right honourable gentleman remarked that those who wished to adopt the policy of Mr. Morley would be mad, or at any rate singularly unwise. If they, in their madness, broke the conapactentered into five years since, how could they guarantee that the more serious national compact would not be broken also, and separation brought about. Under these circumstances he appealed to the House to lend the Govertireent its assistance in passing the measure for which precedence was now asked. Mr. HeunisoN, in supporting Mr. Morley's amendment, asserted that all the prognostications of the hon. member for Cork (Mr. Parnell) had been amply justified by sub- sequent events, and confirmed the report of arl Cow' per's Commission_ As to the National League, it was true as had been stated that the great mjaority of the Irish people looked upon that body as their salvation. Col. Knia-Hsnuart complained of the attacks that had been made on the Irish landlords as einel and unjust. He agreed with Mr. Morley that, Ireland was not dis- organised. On the contrary, it was organised from one end to the other by the National League against this country and in favour of Home Rule. Mr. COSSRAM thought that since the report of the last Commission showed that rents were now In many cases eighteen and twenty per cent, more than they ought to be, the assumption was that the landlords had been making excessive exactions from their tenants. It was the wrong from which they suffered which caused the discontent existing among the Irish people, and he warned the Government that in the course they now proposed to pursue they were only laying the founda- tion for future mischief.
The Speaker having retired for the usual interval, on his return

Mr. CONTI3EAILE called attention to the fact that there was not a quorum, whereupon a "court" was called in the lobbies, and directly 'afterwards members flocked in so rapidly that the Speaker, without counting, an- nom:iced that there were forty present. Mr. FENWICK then spoke in support of Mr. Money's amendmentrefnsing to give his vote for allowing the Government to take precedence with a coercion measure when there were so many measures of an important character haring upon the well-being of the industrial classes that were ripe for solution bY the House. Colonel BLUNDELa,. while urging the Government to petvevere in grappling with the land question, hoped they would also turn their attention to the process of congestion in the population of the British Islands—a congestion that had been fen more severely in Ireland than anywhere, and in producing great pnverty•had also produced much disaffection. He advised that the Government should consider the matter of colonisation, and was enlarging on this point when TIIOASPPAKIIR here-called the hon, member to order as going beyend the subject under discussion. The hon. gentleman concluded by expressing a hope that the Government would proceed with their prorhised remedial measure peri passu with the present bilL Mr. J. E. ELLIS, in supporting the amendment, argued that the real object of the bill for which the Government demanded precedence was to enable the Irish landlords to collect excessive rents.

Mr. U. H. Fowler, Mr. Finlay, and other members fol- lowed, and the debate was adjourned. The report of Supply was brought up and agreed to. The House adjourned at 1125 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. THE COERCION BILL.—Sit GEORGE CAMPBELL resumed the adjourned debate en the Government's motion to give the Irish Crimes Bill precedence over other business.—He was followed by Mr. BRADLAIIGH, who said the Govern- ment had changed their !policy and conduct because they did not know, he would not say their own minds, but the mind of Lord Hartington, who was really charged with conducting the affairs of the nation.—After other members had spoken, Mr. BRYCE urged that a strong case bad not been'made out for urgency, and therefore the Opposition resisted the demand of the Government for the whole time of the House. He saw no prospect of the bill being likely: :10 effect any permanent im- provement in the"".,, position of the Irish people, their minds, or habits. This was our 87th Coer- cion Act, and he did not believe that there ever was a time when a coercion bill was passed ;inrthe House of Commons by a parely party vote.—Mr. Sinclair and Mr. Lockwood followed. The latter was speaking at 5-45, when the debate was adjourned—Mr. W.H. SMITH expressed a strong bops that the discussion upon the motion now before the House would not be unduly prolonged. The matter was one upon which the existence of the Government was at stake, and therefore they desired an early division, on it. He hoped that it would not extend beyond Friday night.— Mr. GLADSTONE would like to see the debate brought to a close at an early period. He was afraid it was not possible to come to any understanding that it would close that night. If the fate of the Government depended upon their bill, that was a reason why a sufficient interval should be allowed for the consideration of it.—Mr. PARNELL stated that five or six, Wish members, including himself, desired to take part in the discussion. . _ _ _ .

The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIIISDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack aborily after four o'clock. THE INDEPENDENCE OF SWAZILAND.—The Earl of Ost- snow stated that the apprehensions of a filibustering expe- dition into Swaziland were not without foundation, and that the subject was now engaging the careful attention of Her Majesty's Government. The Transvaal Government had been informed iw Sir Hercules Robinson that any interfer- ence with the independence of Swaziland without the con- sent of the King would be an infraction of the Convention of 1884.
Their Lordships adjourned at five minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TrtnEsnes.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. TEE COERCION BILL.—The debate on Mr. Smint's mo- tion to give precedence to the Criminal taw Amendment (Ireland) Bill was resumed by Mr. GLADSTONE. The right hon, gentleman, who was received with prolonged Cheers from the Opposition benches, first called attention to the unprecedented position of the House at present, and still more as it would be affected by the adoption of the motion. For two months the independent initiative of the House had been suppressed. He was told that the mode of procedure to be adopted would be the frequent application of the closure rule. He could conceive of no greater calamity to the House. The whole justification of what the Government proposed to do was rested upon what he (Mr. Gladstone) did in 1881. ut in that year the presumptive case of the Government was that Mr. Foreter gave the House full official statements before any demand was made for the surrender of the time of the House; Mr. Gladstone proceeded to point out the fundamental distinction between the present period and 1881. and then asked if it was intended to invite Parliament, under a representative system of government and in a free country, to govern Ireland in defiance of the sentiments and wishes of the vast majority of those whom she sent to re- present her. Dealing with the evidence of Sir R. Buller, the right hon. gentleman said it had been utterly thrown over by the Government, and he insisted that the only legitimate measures for putting down Irish agitation were remedia 1 measures. The Government were going to pursue the old system of dealing with symptoms and neg- lecting causes. Whether they were in a minority or majority, it was important that they should do their duty, and he trusted that they should do it to the last stage of this ill-omened measure, when a fresh blow would be struck, under the name of a Parliamentary statute, at the happiness, the prosperity, and the contentment of Ireland, end at the union with Great Britain. At the close of the right hon. gentleman's speech there was a protracted pause, and the Speaker was about to put the question to the House, when Mr. Chance rose, and the de- bate was continued by that hon. member, who was followed by Mr. Addison, Mr. Menzies, and Mr. Mulhelland.—Mr. Otnsomiz Monchasi said he did his beet to help the passing of the closure, bat it was now evident that the real motive Of the Government in passing it was, not to assure the dignity and efficiency of the House, but to pass a severe Coercion Bill for Ireland.—The House was afterwards ad- dressed by Colonel Sanderson, Mr. Asquith, and Mr. Chain- berlain. berlain, and Mr. Healy.—Mr. SHAW•LEFEVILE moved the ad- journment of the debate. SUPREME COURT OF JUDICATURE (IRELAND) BILL.—The adjourned debate on going into Committee on the above Bill was resumed.—The House went into Committee on the Bill and immediately resumed.—The orders of the day were dis- posed of, and the House adjourned at ten minutes past two.

An applicaiion was Made in the London Bankruptcy Court on Monday to appoint a special manager to the estate of It. A. and John Stewart, timber-merchants, of London and, New Brunswick, who have failed with, it is stated, liabilities amounting to £lOO,OOO. 'The applica- tion was refused.

At Whitechapel County Court, William Macdonald has obtained £4O damages from the North Metropolitan Tramway Company as compensation for injuries sus- tained through being knocked down and run over by one of the defendant company's cars. Early on Monday morning, one of the porters at the Shettlestone passenger railway station, near Glasgow, observed a man hanging from the Post-bridge, and, going-up to him, saw that he was quite dead. The de- ceased had his dinner near him, and bad evidently been going to his work. The Queen will hold a review at Aldershot on the 9th \ of July. The force will be composed of regulars, and volunteers. Further details will be communicated to the general officers commanding. The volunteer corps in and abmt London will march past her Majesty at Etrekinghtun Palace on the 2nd of July. - justice Smith, hi. the Queen's Bench, on Mottft.; gave judgment in ;the case of the Queen V. Sandoval. Col. Sand Oval was found guilty a few weeks ago of a breach of the Foreign Enlistment Act. A light engine came into collision on Saturday on the South Tottenham /ine with the 4 55 am. workmen's train from South Tottenha.m to London, near Harringay Park Station. Five persons were injured. The injured were lemoved to their homes, after having their wounds dressed. One of the injured was sent to the Tottenham Havdtal, and another to the Metropolitan Free Hospital. The line was blocked four hours.

At Worship-street Police-court, on Monday, James ifinemore, 49, of Paul-street, Finsbury., was charged with tialling his -wife on Saturday. The prisoner appeared nervous and distressed. Evidence was given by the Iconstable who arrested Finernore, on the information of Iltaereighbour, and who obtained particulars of what had I occurred from the prisoner himself. A remand was ordered for eight days. An application to allow the money and other valuables found on the prisoner to be. I landed to his friends was refused.

WIFE Manna IN Losnox.—On Sunday afternoon Jas. Tmemore, collar dresser, returned to his house, 94, Paul- street, Fin.shuu, under the influence of drink, and began quarrelling with his wife As, however, they quarrelled very frequently, other people living in the house took no notice. Later on Plnemore called a Mrs. .ater into the room and pointed to his wife, who was lying in a pool of .:blood, bleeding from a wound in the stomach. Fine- more afterwards said be had stabbed his wife and that it wafi her own fault. The woman was taken to-the hos- pital, but died on the way. Finemore is in custody. _ .

SHOCKING Muuotat THROUGH A WIFE'S MISCONDUCT.— A shocking murder was committed at Wombwell Junction, near Barnsley, on Sunday, by Isaac Haztehurst, .a collier. Hazlehurst had a number of men drinking at his house, he fetching the drink from a palalic house. Returning with scsne liquor he missed his wife from the room, and, going upstairs, found her with one of the party, named Leather. He tamed Leather out, and then kicked his wife about the head. In the morning she was found dead. Haziehurst was arrested and taken before the magistrates, and was remanded on a charge of wilful murder.

DEATH MOH DYDROPITOBTA.—A wry sad case of bydro- phobia has just occurred at Hathern, Leicestershire. It •appears that a boynamed Frederick White, aged 13 years, was bitten on the face by a stray terrier on the 16th February. The.dnot, showed'tunmstakable signs of madness, and the father of the lad pursued it, and suc- ceeded in kiliingit. The boy was placed under medical care, but decided symptoms of hydrophobia were mini- fested,..and he grew gradually worse and died in great agony. This is the first case in the county since June, 1885,- when two men who were bitten by a stray dog died within a few days of each other.

Exrstran-s Susar-Wortarnra.—An extraordinary case of sheep-worrying has been reported to the Shropshire police. Mr. James Keatley, farmer, of High Hatton Hall, Hodnett, who keeps several hundred sheep, having missed a large number, communicated with Superinten- dent Rowlands, of Shrewsbury, and on inspection being made OR the farm 22 dead sheep were found in a ditch, where they had evidentiy ran through fright, and were suffocated Thirty-two more of the flock were found' bitten or otherwise badly injured. The entire loss, which is very great, has to be sustained by the farmer. A mad dog has been found in the district. . GREAT Fins ra Lrrimpoot.—On Saturday afternoon, about three o'clock, a. fire was discovered in a warehouse situate in Green-street, Victoria-road, Liverpool. The steam fire engines, on arriving at the burning building, which Was of six storeys, set to wsrrk, but the dense volumes of smoke prevented them doing much to check the progress of the flames which spread to the entire Wilding. By seven o'clo:it the roof fell In, and it was not till 10 o'clock that the fire was mastered. The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth storeys were !Merit out, and damage was done to the amount of £25,030. The build- ing contained a-large quantity of American cotton. THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE AND METHODISM—MUNIFICENT Girrs..--SiE W. Mc. arthur, who had previously undertaken to contribute £lO,OOO for the erection of a home for ministers daughters in connection with the Wesleyan College at Belfast, has just made a conditional promise of Pii,ooo more towards the same object, it having been ' I found that, in addition to what is now available, a ' capital fund of £lO,OOO is board and education. for the pupils. The vice-president I of the Conference suggests that such a fund would be required in order to provide the very best Jubilee fund of Irish Methodism, and goes on to say that if the Irish Methodists undertake to raise £5,000, Sir William Me. Arthur will be prepared to give 1'5,000 in addition to his former mtmificent'd,onation. In view of this generous offer, it is stated tirA the Other Jubilee proposals have been withdrawn. THE Da TOURVILLE Mrs-run-v.—The petition in the matter of the Brigham estates for the appointment of a receiver came before Mr. Justice Kay on Saturday morning, but was ordered to stand over until next Saturday. It is alleged that young De Tourville, who, if alive, is entitled to the estates, is dead, a body resembling .his having been found on the shore of the Bay of Naples. Counsel appeared for the guardian ad litem' when Mr. Justice Kay inquired how such guardian could have been appointed by the court, as Ordex;l3, Rule 1, laid it down that the infant for whom the guardian is required should have been. previous)), served with notice of the application for appointment. An affidavit of a. chartered accountant at Manchester was handed up to his lordship, who, seeing that the requirements of the said rule and order were complied with, adjourned the case, remarking that he should require the fullest explanation how the gentleman:could have sworn the child had been served when he knew the child was dead.
