Several of the special juries engaged in bearing record ewes at the Clonmel Assizes, have given the usual fee of one guinea to Mrs. Hanlon, mother of the man killed in the recent encounter-vrith the -police at Youghal. On Sunday Morning, eight young men, of the _farming class, were arrested.at Clokher, county Kerry, for attack- ing the house of 'John Feahan, near Killarney, and threatening him last St. Stephen's Day. One of the party had turned informer. _ _

Duty on Monday therlead bodies of two men named Finn and Grant, were found in the &ingrate briekwerks, Belfast. It appears that while under the influence of drink the men had sat down beside one of the kanes to warm themselves,and having fallen asleep were itephy- xiated by the fumes of the biuning-bricks.

John Wilson was found guilty on Saturday at the Downpatrick Assizes, for having feloqiously killed and slain James Curran, at the Queen's Island, Bedfast, on the 4th June last, on the occasion of the attack on the -navvies, when Curran was driven into Belfast Lough and drowned. Sentenced to seven years' penal servi- tude. William Holland and William Fisher were indicted for alike offence, and were acquitted. Private Edgeworth, sth Dragoon Guards, whose-arrest on Saturday night, in Belfast, for using party expres- sions, which led to rather serious rioting, during which several policemen were severely injured, was, at the police-court, sentenced to two months' imprison- ment, Pour of the other six prisoners arrested were lined 40s. and costs, while two ringleaders named Kidd and Hyde were respectively sentenced to three and six months' hard labour.

The divorce suit instituted by the Hon. Ann White against the Hon. Robert White came on in the Dublin Divorce Court on Monday. The petitioner-sought tore- wit the time for the respondent's answer to the suit, and asked for an alimonyof £4OO a year. It was stated that the petitioner was in want of means, and the case was adjourned-to allow of evidence to prove that there is a mortgage of £16,000 on Lord Bantry's estate vested in the respondent About ten p.m., on ',Sunday, a police patrol from 'rra- lee, consisting or a sergeant and two men, was in ambush at Ballybrenagh„near the house of a man named .King, when a. party of moonlighters approached, and entered the house. The police were about to follow, when one of the gang, stationed outside to keep watch, gave the alarm, and the whole party nine in number, rushed out. The police came forward, and the sergeant called on the men in the Queen's name to halt ; but the only reply was'for two of them to turn and fire at the patrol. The police returned the fire, and one of the moonlietters turned back towards the house, exclaiming "I am shot," and almost immediately fell dead. The police pursued tbe-ethers, but in the darkness they escaped over some liehla. On returning, the patrol found the dead man was Patrick Linehan), 'of Breunom, a district notorious for moonlighting.

The two police officers against whom a coroner's jury have returned a verdict of murder in respect of the fatal affray at Youghal were on Wednesday removed in custody to Qeeenstown. It is announced that General Sankey, chairman of the Irish Board of Works, has been appointed Under Secretary for Ireland in succession to Sir Redvers Buller. The general is a Tipperary man. On Thursday, at the Antsim Assizes at Belfast, Charles Cushley was indicted for having killed Eliza Cameron during one of the riots in Belfast in last August. The jury were unable to agree, and were discharged. Judge Boyd sat in the Dublin Bankruptcy Court, on Wed- nesday, for the examination of Father Ryan, in the matter of Thomas Moroney, bankrupt, now in Kilinainharn Gaol for refusing to give evidence. Service of summons on Father Ryan was proved, but the rev, gentleman did not appear, neither did two other witnesses. Warrants were issued for their apprehension. FATHER KELLER COMMITTED TO GAOL—The case of Patrick O'Brien, a tenant on the Ponsonby estate, who adopted the Plan of Campaign, and was afterwards adjudi- cated a bankrupt,was listed on Saturday, before Judge Boyd, for examination of witnesses. Among the witnesses sub- pcened was the Rev Daniel Keller, of Youghal, who, refus- ing to obey the mandate of the court, was arrested and taken to Dublin on Friday. in charge of two court messengers. Judge Boyd sat at 12 o'clock. Long before that hour the en- trances to the Court were blocked by a larae crowd evident- ly anxious to obtain admission. Father Keller arrived at 12 o'clock precisely. He was accompanied by the Lord Mayor, Dr Kenny, M.P., Mr O'Connor, M.P., and Mr Wm. O'Brien, and followed by a large cheering crowd. Arch- biehop Walsh was amongst those who were accommodated with seats in court. Father Keller said the question put to him would have a tendency to elicit an answer which would disclose matters of which he had become cognisant as a priest, and he could riot make any such disclosure. Judge Boyd said that was no legal justification for refusing to answer the question. He then directed the registrar to make out a warrant for the committal of Father Keller to gaol. The official shorthand writer having transcribed his notes of the evidence, Fathereeller signed the statement as accurate, and he was then taken into custody by Archibald Ellis, the court messenger, who drove off with him to Kil- main ham Gaol. A large crowd followed the cab the entire way, cheering Father Keller. Mr Harrington, M.P., Dr Kenny, M.P., and Mr Wiliam O'Brien also drove to the prison, where the crowd remained cheering for some time.

div.head: NEW CHURCH LECTURES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: NEW CHURCH LECTURES AT WARRINGTON.

Another of this series of lectures was given in the Cairo-street Schoolroom, on Monday evening, by the Re+. H. Cameron; subject "The early chap- ters of Genesis and the fall of man." The subject, the lecturer said, of the early chapter of Genesis, in which We have an account of the fall of man, seems. to have been one of the subjects that had comman- ded the attention of learned men and reflective men in this age. They were all very well aware that the early chapters of Genesis cannot be uncle)). stood as literal history. At least that was 'the be- lief of most of our theologians who had written on the subject in modern times. It had been gener- ally supposed that the creation was completed in six days, because the early chapters of Genesis spoke of something being formed during six days, and that God rested on the seventh day. But now most commentators declared that these days are not to be understood as literal ones, and that they might signify and denote ages, or states of the world's development or formation. They would see from that that it was a total departure from a mere literal reading of the early chapters of Genesis. There were many statements iii those chapters that they could not understand literally, anduurely that of the third chapter that Ged .formed Adam and Eve, placed them in the garden of Eden, and set before there the "tree of knowledge," which they were not to eat of, was one of these. Could they suppose for one moment to God, if he made man pure and innocent, would place him in a garden and put before him a tree which he was not to eat of. One would naturally suppos3 that if God did not want man to have partaken of this fatal tree he would not have put it there, for what was the use of putting the tree there. Then it involved the idea that death and life grew upon trees. They knew nothing about such trees as these. They knew trees which, if they partook of, would poison a man, but Adam did not die, and we read that he lived upward of 900 years. Then they • heard of a talking serpent that appeared before the woman and beguiled her. He wished to show them that they had something brought before them in these early chapters of Genesis that was of far more con- sequence for them to know than that which the literal reading of the history would give. Emma- nuel Swedenborg, who had written a great deal on that subject, and who had also, as he (the lecturer) I believed, been,enlightened on the subject by the I Spirit of GM, told us that what the serpent ' denotes is the general principle of the sensual nature of man. It was described as being the most subtle of the beasts of the field, and men were tempted by their sensual natures in the most seductive and subtle forms. When they yielded to these seductions they were led astror by the wiles of the serpent. By reading the early chapters of Genesis in this sense they were put upon their guard against the seductions of the serpent—their own sensual nature—and also directed to look to the great serpent bruiser, the Lord Jesus Christ. In reply to a question put by a person present, the lecturer explained that he did net look upon the history of the book of Genesis as being a literal his- tory, but a symbolic one. When we understood its symbolic meaning, we would find that all scientific and free-thinking objections to the Word of God were cleared away. The further we go back in the history of the race, the more did we find this sym- bclic writing, and it is the most powerful writing of all. He looked upon Genesis as being are inspired allegorical , history, and the very fact that it was said that life and death grew upon a tree, and that there was a talkinp serpent, showed that the book was allegorical. One or two other questions were asked and answered, and the meeting was then closed with a prayer.

—tow Salisbury is suffering from an influenza cold, itds believed, he contracted on Wednesday last. Thernalady is naming its normal course, and occasions no anxiety to his lordship's family. Sir Win_ienner visited Lord Salisbury on Sunday, and pronounced that he was doing well, and in a fair way towards speedy MCOVery. A MEMBER RECEIVING HIS MAaCHING ORDERS.—At a meeting on Saturday of the Liberal Council of the Colas Valley Division, the attitude of Mr. IL F. Beaumont,..M.P., on the Irish question was discussed. A proposal thatthe hon. gentleman should be informed that there was no intention to bring him forward again, met with no seconder, but resolutions were passed expressing un- abated confidence in Mr. Gladstone and appointing a committee to select a candidate who would support the right hon. gentleman's Irish policy.

THE LTEHRAL LEADERS AND MR. CHAMERALAIN.—MT. Chamberlain, acknowledging a resolution adopted by a Liberal meeting at Dudley, says he sincerely shares the hope it expresses of an early agreement amongst the Liberal leaders. He suggests that party organisations would do much at pres-nt to bring about reunion by a serions'and impartial discussion of points of difference. In his Birmingham speech, Mr. Chamberlain adds, he endeavoured to summarise the objections to Mr. Glad- stone's proposals, and he believes that if these points were fairly discussed by Liberal organisations there would be found a large and general agreement. Mn. BRIGHT AND IRELAND.—MT. Bright, in a letter to a Birmingham correspondent, states that his sympathy for Ireland is as strong AS ever, and he is anxious to do justice to her people, but it is this sympathy which makes it impossible for him to consent to hand overthe government of five millions of the Queen's subjects to a "rebel conspiracy," of whom he cannot doubt but that two millions are loyal and content. The right hon. gentleman expresses the opinion that forty members of the Irish party are supported by the dollars contributed by the avowed enemies of England on the American continent.

Mr. Davitt, addressing a meeting of Irishmen on Mon- day night, at Glasgow, said the Irish leaders were dd,- notrnced by Lord Salisbury for their want of exalted patriotism. The Marquis and his party would hang the Irish leaders to-morrow if they appealed to the arbitra- ment of the sword and did not win, as the revolutionists of Italy and Hungary did in past generations. Quack statesmen Hite Mr. Chamberlain had tried for many years to give measures of Westminster medicine, but discontent still existed in Ireland, and it would be- come stronger and nam embarrassing to England.and more formidable in its representations to the House of Commons until Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule scheme-was granted. The spoon-feeding process to Ireland had been a hideous failure. -Though the prisons were filled with Irish patriots, and even with priests, the Irish would fight on till Home Rule was won.

div.head: DEPUTATIONS TO MINISTERS.'
div.p: DEPUTATIONS TO MINISTERS.'

Baron .H. Do Worms, Parliamentary secretary to thu. BoanlefeTrade, received a deputation from the northern counties with reference to the Railway Rates Bill on day. They They advocated, in connection with the working '1 of certain local railways, the retention of sub-section 2 of the 25th clause of he bill. Baron de Worms referred the deputation to the views already expressed by the President of the Board of Trade on the subject. Mr. Stanhope received a deputation of volunteer mem- bers of Parliament, at the War Office, on Monday, on the question of the capitation grant. Mr. Stanhope was accompanied by Lord Harris and General Fremantle. The deputation thought it would be disadvantageous to the force if the capitation grant of 355. depended solely upcn shooting. Various suggestions were made, which Mr. Stanhope said should receive his-careful attention.

A deputation introduced by Mr. Morley, M.P., waited upon Baron Henry De Worms, parliamentary secretary of the Board of Trade, at the House of Commons, on Mon- day, to advocate the establishment of an organisation which should control patent agents. It was urged that the existing Institute of patent agents was competent for this purpose, and thedeputation recommended that it should be endowed with a charter for the purpose.' Baron De.Wonns, in reply, said he would lay the views of the deputation before the President of the Board of Trade. He pointed out that in thoxvi....t of -the Patent Committee a somewhat similar suggestion to dhat now made was embodied. 1

A deputation of members of Parliament and, others waited upon Lord Cranbrook, at the Education Depart- ment, on Monday afternoon; to urge upon him the neces-i sity of Government action with regard to technical education. Mr. Mundella introduced the deputation, and said they desired that the' Government should give school boards and local authorities increased power-to promote industrial an technical classes, and that these should be put under the Science and Art Department. Sir Lyon Playfair, Sir R. Temple, Mr. George Dixon, Pro- fessor Stuart, and others having, spoken, Lord Cranbrook said it was not possible3n the office which be held, to reach the objects desired. That must be done by legislation. Without tusking any declaration of policy, he would say, that he saw no objectian to localities acting themselves so as to bring about a system of technical education most suited to them. On these points he would consult with his colleagues, and see what could be done.

making of the Canal; and, if the waterway itself should prove successful, competition for the carriage of goods will put them in a splendid position. They can consequently afford to risk much in order to gain much ; and if they flock to the scheme in sufficient numbers they can command a trade which will ensure interest on the original outlay. Then, as the circular notes, there are "the landowners whose property will be required for the Canal." They, too, are especially in- terested not only in taking " part pay) , ment in shares," but in making every effort to assist in raising the capital required. It is a matter of course to say in the first place that they will receive a good price for such slices of land as they will be called upon to sell ; and it is equally a matter of course to observe that, if the Canal be made, it will add considerably to the value, of every acre of land upon its margin. Land- owners ought to become liberal subscribers because they have reason to hope for a liberal return. But the main consideration, after all, is the likelihood. or otherwise, of the Ship Canal undertaking being in itself a profitable investment. On this head we have the con- fident opinions Of min who, entering into an inquiry as sceptics, have come out thorough believers. Some of these men are now on the Board, and they are backing their opinion with their money. If this feeling is general amongst the capitalists of Lancashire, and Cheshire, the three millions wilier) will be required will be subscribed by August next ; but if, on the other hand, investors are too much " sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought," this enterprise of greatest pith and moment " will lose the name of action."

THE question of making provision for technical education in this country is gradu- ally coming to the front, but it does not by any means as yet obtain the attention which the importance of the subject demands. A good elementary education is now being given to the children in our national schools; but, except in large or specially favoured centres of population, little or nothing is be- ing done to ensure that when they become artizans they shall be skilled artizans in the full sense of the term. This is not so on the Continent; the elementary school, the free library, and the technical school are found side by side, and the result is, as Professor ROSCOE says, that "on the Continent the progress in technical, industrial, scientific, and commercial education during the past ten years has been enormous." There are some who argue that there is a tendency to "overdo it" in the matter of education, but that can hardly be said to be the case with England, so long as we are so much behind other counties. The Englishman is usually ready enough to put himself forward as equal to any foreigner in the matter of either fighting or working; and past experience justifies him in his confidence. But why should he not be equally ready to boast that he can bring as much intelligence to his work? Muscle counts for a great deal, but mind counts for more in these days of steam and electricity. There is nosstanding still ; the nation that does not go forward, Sand at a good pace, too, will be left in the Tear. And that means "foreign competition' in its worst form; orders going abroad which should be executed at home; with less work and reduced wages ; for it is in the nature of things that in the long run good orders will go to the good workers. Having an eye to all this, a large deputation of members of Parliament waited, on Monday, upon Lord CRAUBROOTC, as President of the Council of Education. The necessity for oomething be- ing done, and done quickly, was urged with great force by various speakers.; but they did not meet with much encouragement. Lord CRANBROOK pleaded that, "whatever might be the feeling of the public, Parliament itself had not really pronounced on,the subject of technical education." This ivquite true,-and it should now be the business of the people to insist that their representativessehall take action in the matter. Something can be done locally where the public spirit is active and intelli- gent; but unfortunately efforts of this kind are-irregular and spasmodic. 'What is needed is that the State, in some form or other, shall givefinancial support—such, for instance, as is accorded in the way of grants for elemen- tary,education. We spend million upon mil- lion with the greatest facility when it is a matter of making provision for maiming or killing-men, but when it is a question of en- suing that there shall be an intelligent mind in a sound body there is tusually a long wrangle over sixpences. We must try to re- form this, and "reform it altogether." As Longfellow has beautifully expressed it : Were half the power that fills the world with torpor, Were half the wealth bestowed on camps and courts, Civen to redeem the human mind from error, •There‘were no need for arsenalstnor forts.

AFTER much discussion and many meetings, something like an understanding has been arrived at, in Warrington, as to what are to be the ochief features of the celebration of the QuEEN's,jubilee. There is to be a monstre procession of trades, friendly societies, school children, and inhabitants, and atreat to the aged poor. The wall in Sankey-street, in front of the Town Hall, is to be taken down; the land is tote suitably laid out,.and there is to be a handsome fountain erected, the cost of swhich Sir GILI3ERT GRBENALL has generously promised to defray. A sub-com- mittee of the 'Jubilee Committee ,has been appointed, tog, to confer with the Library and Muoeum Committee with the object of 1 making .arrangements for converting the Library into a Free Lending Library as part of the Jubilee celebration. We believe this can be done, and that it ought to be done: for it is a .project which as met with the approval not only of the limited circle called together by the Mkrzoß but by a Town's Meeting of the inhabitants. Indeed, it was all but first favourite at the meeting held in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, and, if it had not been felt that it would be ungracious to refuse the gift of a fountain, it is probable that it would have displaced the proposal for laying out the land in front of the Town Hall. As it was, the Libmry scheme obtained the hightest number of votes when there were three proposals under considera- tion; and it was no more than seven behind when the final vote was taken. It is as well, perhaps, that it did not distance every competitor at this meeting, because, as the matter now stands, we shall, in all likelihood, "knock down the wall," as the phrase is, and at the same time free the Library. There is a strong feeling in the town in favour of establishing a Technical School, as was shown by the voting on Mon- day night, and there is another large section of ratepayers who think that the Public Baths should be enlarged and improved at the earliest opportunity. If this was not "the day of small things," so far as War-

div.head: EXAMINthi, SATURDAY, MARCH 26, 1887
div.p: THE EXAMINthi, SATURDAY, MARCH 26, 1887

rington is concerned, there is no reason why, all the four schemes should not be carried out. Mr. THOMAS MORRIS started out some time ago to find one hundred gentlemen who would contribute one hundred pounds each to a Jubilee Fund, with a view to carrying out several projects in good style, but he met with checks rather than cheques, and so turned aside in despair. Sir GILBERT GREENALL set a bad example by confining his Jubilee Gift to one sect; but he has made amends in some degree by the promise of a fountain to the town, which will, we have reason to believe, be a credit alike to the borough and the borough member. It was natural that the Conservatives who were at the MAYOR'S meeting on Monday should vote for taking down the wall and secur- ing the founta;n particularly as the project will result in edorning the front of the Con- servative Club, as well as the front of the Town Hall. It was not in human nature to I resist the appeal of the MAYOR and of the BOROUGH MEMBER, conjoined as it was with the interests of propetty owners—to say nothing of a taste for the ornamental—and we are inclined to think that, under similar circumstances, the Liberals would have acted in a similar manner. As it happens, how- ever, they were uader no te nptation ; they favoured, as is usual with them, educational projects ; and they may fairly ask—now that the Conservatives are having their way as to "the wall "—that a helping hand shall be given in the effort that is to be made to free the Library. Not, of course, that the diffu- sion of literature is a matter of party politics; it is happily beyond and above them ; and e are glad to think that, from the QUEEN downward, there is a growing desire amongst all classes to brighten, and beautify, and re- fine the lives of the poorest by increasing the facilities for their acquaintance with the wisest men of all ages and of all nations.

What is it that the •‘ Knights and Dames of the Primrose League " do when they come together in " habitation ?" From the newspaper reports, the League would seem to "give a local habitation and a name to airy nothing." There seems to have been a gar- den party at Grappenhall ; and we hear of a meeting at Wilderspool Brewery. Can it have been a case of " fuddle and feed ?" It is satisfactory, at any rate, to know that Mr. Seel, of Southport, will " from time to time visit them, to see that they are going on properly." By-the-by, who is Mr. Seel ? Is he a policeman ?

There was an all-night sitting of the House of Commons on Monday night, which lasted till half-past one on Tuesday afternoon. People who "make a night of it," whether legislators or costermongers, generally get to talking very freely. It is not surprising, therefore, to learn that one member was re- ported to the chair for speaking of another as drunk, or that a third M.P. threatened to give a fellow-member "two lovely black eyes ''—as the song has it. Mr. Balfour, however, lapsed into the language of so- briety, and told the truth when he said "the Government was paralysed." It is paralysed.'

Aressrs. Duncan and Spratt, of Manchester, give some figures highly suggestive of the need of the Ship Canal. Referring to their importation of a certain lot of produce, they say :—" The gross weight was 803 tons. Freight and insurance from Boston, U.S.A., to the Mersey £26 4s rid ; Liverpool Dock and town dues, master. porterage, &c., £l6 Ss 9d; cartage in Liverpool, £5 os 4d; car- riage from Liverpool to Manchester (station to station), £3l zs 4,1 ; therefore it costs twice as much from the Mersey to Man- chester as it does from Boston. U.S.A , to the Mersey. thus demonstrating the ex- ceptional cheapness of water carriage."
NEW Canromc Cnortot ar WlDNES.—Gronnel is being marked out ott Waterloo-road for the erection of a new Catholic Church, and building operations will be commenced

forthwith. ZION CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The anneal missionary ser- mons ia connection with Zion Methodist Free Church, Widnes, were preached on t•unday by the Rev. A. Hands, of Liverpool. On Monday evening a public meeting Was held under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Snape, and several interesting addresses were delivered. The choir sang a number of anthems under the conductorship of Mr. J. Bet- ney. The collections realised a good SUM DRINKING, &C., AT RUNCORN.—At the RUM= Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. G. L. Davies, John Welsh was committed to gaol for seven days for begging.—Robert Sumner, for being drunk in Trentham-street, was lined 5s and costs.—On Thursday, at the same court, before Mr. John fitundrit, Henry Smith, for begging in Percival-lane, was sent to prison for seven days.—For a similar offence in Bridge-street, Thomas Lunt was committed for fourteen

days. RUNCORN' GYMNASMIL—The members of the Runccrn Gymnasium en Thursday night competed in the seini-linal round for the District Challenge Shield against the Liver- pool Victoria Gymnasium, a club which has been in exist- ence for e iveral years, the competition taking place at the St. Augustine's gchool-roona, Saliebury-s., Liverpool. The points scored were Victoria, 231; Runcorn, 2051-, the visitors thus losing by 25i points. Messsrs. Milner and

Boote acted as judges. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE AND SIREET OBSTRUCTION AT RUNCORN.—Ht Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Wm. Donbabin, a youth, was charged with obstructing the foot- path in Regent•street.—P.C. butherland proved the case. Superintendent Hollingworth observed upon the annoyance this practice caused, and the Chief Constable, who occupied a seat on the hence, remarked that he had given instruc- tions for the offence to be put down. Only that morning he saw men and boys standing on a footpath, and a gentleman had to go in the roadway.—A. fine of 6d and costs, 03 6d, was imposed. EXTENSIVE THEFTS BY A RUNCORN YOUTH.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph A. Ward, a youth 15 years of age, was charged on remand with stealing two car- digan jackets, two fronts, four necktics, a shirt, a handker- chief, and a cap, value 10s, the property of Messrs Egerton and Co., hatters, Bridge-street. He was further charged , with having stolen five briarwood pipes and four packs of playing cards, belonging to Mrs. Phoebe Dunn, stationer. Bridge-street; and also with stealing two fronts and a neck- tie, the property of Peter Noon, clothier, Church-street.— Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, Widnes. appeared for the prisoner, and pleaded guilty. He delivered an address to the Bench in mitigation of the offence that elicited appre- ciative applause in court.—Mr. Henry Reynolds did not wish to send the prisoner to goal, and fined him £2, or in default 14 days' hard labour. The money was paid. ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr H Ciaskell, junior, Thomas Longshaw, labourer, of Warrington, was charged with stealing two spades, seven sacks, and a coat, value 28s, the property of Edward Percy, contractor, Victoria-street. The prisoner pleaded gnilty. Be bad stolen the articles whllst in the employ of Mr Percy. and had disposed of them to Mr Sim- bock, marine store dealer, Appleton-street, and to Thomas Jones, forge roller, of Philip-street, Warrington. The pri- soner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.— James Guire, a youth, nos charged with stealing a bun 'loaf from the shop of Mr El N Wharton, grocer, Church- : street. Mrs Wharton saw the robbery committed, and the prisoner was pursued and captured by Police Constable I Houghton. The prisoner had only recently been liberated from a reformatory, where he had served a term of five years, and he was committed to the Quarter Sessions for

l " tria . • Ac rum Fan SLANDER. AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, at Widnes County Court, before his Honour Judge T. P. K. Thomp- son and a special jury, Mrs. Ann Roberts, of Cow-lane, Ditton, brought an action agtinst Osorge Yates, a weigher, formerly a blacksmith, of the aims place, to recover £5O for alleged slander. The case had been remitted from the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, Liverpool Registry. Mr. Longton, of Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Thomas Swift, barrister, St. Helens (instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles), defended. Mr. Swift disclaimed any imputation upon the charac- ter of the plaintiff, and said if that admission •had been made sooner a satisfactory arrangement might have been arrived at. At the suggestion of his Honour the counsel retired, but were unable to come to an amicable de- cision.—Mr. Langton then stated the terms of the slander, and described the injury done to the plaintiff in causing her lodgers to leave her roof.—Mr. Swift contended that tire words used did not constitute slander, and the Judge being of the same opinion, Mr. Langton withdrew the case. I Each side was ordered to pty its own costs. RuNcoart COuNTY CoaßT.—His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes held a sitting ef this court on Tuesday, when there were set down for hearing one adjourned plaint, 117 original i plaints, 5 default summonses, and 22 judgment summonses. I —James Dunbobio, farmer' Weston, claimed from Maria Somerville, wife of David Somerville, the sum of 103., for damages alleged to have been done by the defendant's fowls trespassing on plaintiff's land. The sum ef ss. was claimed , from Thomas Roberts under similar circumstances.—Mr. Lake appeared for the defendants.—The son of the plaintiff admitted that the trespass had taken place early in the past year, and also in the summer, and he had had the damage to the potatoes assessed without giving notice to the defend- ants.—His Honour said persons keeping hens were bound to fence them in and keep them of their neighbours' land, or make themselves liable to an action for any damage they did. As the evidence as to the damage in the case was so ' unsatisfactory, he should only give nominal damages of 2s. against Mrs. Somerville, and Is. against Roberts If Mrs. Somerville bad no separate estate execution must be stayed until she had.

MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES.—The an- nual Congregational tea party was held on Thursday even- ing. About 130 persons partook of the repast, which was proyided in Malin's Temperance Hall, the tables being seperintended by Mesdames Lewes, E Hirst, J Doming, W Horning, Chapman, Guise, Teesdale, Shepherd, Scott, Poole, and W liodgkinson; and Mines Barton, Thomas, A Baron, and E Warne. Subsequently a concert was given in Milton Chapel, under the presidency of Captain Brunner, and there was a capital attendance. The Chairman delivered an sppropriate address, and in the course of the evening Mr. Whitfield, the secretary, pre- sented an encouraging report. Mr J Poole, the con- ductor of the choir, had arranged an admirable pro- gramme, in which he also took part, the vocalists being Miss Poole (Sandbach), Mrs. Poole, Miss Sirnkin (Runcorn), Miss B Poole, and Mies Travis; and Messrs T Gibson and A Fax (Runcorn). The chief interest centred in the appearance of Miss Poole, who has now joined the ranks of the profes- sionals, and she bids fair to achieve a reputation even greater than her early efforts indicated. The full rich tones of her highly cultured soprano voice, aided by artistic ex- pression, were heard to great advantage in the songs she fiad chosen, and she was enthusiastically encored. The other vocalists were also very successful, and Mr .1 Jones per- formed a pianoforte solo with much skill. The selections of the Vocal Union, under the leadership of Mr J Davies. contributed considerably to the enjoyment of those present. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.—On Thursday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and T. Sutton Timm's, Amos Percival, of Gossaee-street, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the supplrt of his son Charles. aged 14 years, who is AR inmate of the Stockport Industrial School. An order had been made upon the defendant to pay 2s per week by the magistrates of Oldbury, near Bir- mingham, and it was proved that he was now in a position to pay. The defendant objected to making the payment because he had discovered that his son, instead of being taught a trade, was sent oat hawking "pots." The Bench made an order for the payment of Is 61 per week.— Frederick Bounds, a barman, was summoned for using threatening language to William Kay, a breakaman em- ployed at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson. The magis- trates dismissed the case.—James Itawlinson, Michael Allen' Michael Fitzeimmons, and Mary Tracy were each fined for drunkenuess.—An old woman named Sarah Jarvis, of Water-street, was boand over to be of good behaviour for creating a breach of the -peace.—Mr. G. H. Hanby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—Miles Grant, Joseph Newton, Lawrence Murray, George Whitby, Edward Lightfoot, Edward Bearden, Charles McKenna, John Mur- phy, John Dugan, John Hindley, James Houghton, John Daley. Samuel Greeman, and Edward Ryan. The usual fine of 5s was imposed in each ClB6.—nomas Eddowes, farm labourer. Ditton, was committed to goal for seven days. for refusing to pay a poor rate of 88 6(1 to the over- seers of that township. TEE ALLEGED RORBERI OF COPPER AT WIDNES.--At Widnes Police Court on Monday, before Mr. G. Pilkingron, Owen Kerley and Thomas Smith, of Widnes, and Patrick Hanlon, of Warrington, were charged on remand with hav- ing, on or about the Ist met, at Widnes, stolen 4901 be of copper, worth £9, the property (1 the London and North Western Railway Company. George Christopher Howard, marine store dealer, of Warrington, was charged with re- ceiving the copper knowing it to have been stolen. Mr. ' Preston, of Liverpool, prosecuted for the bampany, and Mr. I, A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, defended Howard, who had been released on bail. The evidence given was similar ' to thit published in this journal last week, and showed that .356 ingots of copper, weighing Mout a cwt each were consigned by the St. Helens Copper Company per the Lon- don aLd North Western Railway to West Bank Dock to the order of the St. Helens and Liverpool Lighter. age Company. When the metal was being transferred to the hold of the steamship Warrington it was discovered that four begets were missing. Next morning Alfre I Mercer, carter, of Davies-street, was engaged by Kerley to convey some "iron "to Warrington, and he was accompanied be Kerley and S:nith, by whom, with the assistance of harden, the eopver was disposed of to the prisoner How ,rd. Toe traneaction, as described by Kerley to Inspector Wood, was AS fOIIOWS :—" I saw the prisoner Howard and his father at Warrington the night before the copper was taken from Widnes. I told him I had some copper, and they told me to bring it. I took it on the following day and again saw the prisoner Howard and his father. They looked at the copper and said they would not have it until it was cut up. The copper was then taken to Davies, the tinsmith. After it wan cut up Howard would not have it. I then told Han- lon to make the bast of it. The prisoner Howard then gave me 4, on Friday as a (Rib, and on Saturday Warburton gave me 355. Smith knows nothing about it." Warburton is a, servant of Howard's.—The prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for triel, and Howard was again admitted to bail.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

- - - "Come gentle spring, etherial mildness, come;" and be quick about it, or the year will be gone. The poet who began the other day, " Hail, smiling morn," was in the right vein; for it did hall, and then it snowed, and thawed, and was altogether bad.

The Rev. George Bond has done well to retire from the threatened contest for a seat on the Widnes Local Board. The electors have had some experience of him as a mem- ber of the School Board; and if the issue had been put to them—" Bond" or "Free ?" they would have voted to be free from bond.

In the House of Lords, last night, Lord alisbury said " a return to Protection was not within the range of political policies." What will the Fair Traders do now? Will they recognise that they are " sat upon" by a Tory Premier ? Or will they squirm, and demand that the Government shall be turned out?

Father Keller is not quite cat off from the luxuries, or shall we say necessaries of life ? He has been asking for snuff, and has been allowed to have it. He has shown all along that he was up to snuff; but it cannot, after this, be said that he doesn't care a pinch for coercion.

In view of the fact that so many towns are about to celebrate the Queen's jubilee by establishing Free Libraries, Mr. Thos. Green- wood has issued a shilling edition of his work on the subject. It brings all information on Free Libraries down to date, and is altogether a capital work. It is published by Messrs. Simpkin, Marshall, and Co., London.

Walking Day in Warrington will, in all likelihood be postponed this year to jubilee week. It would be rather too much of a good thing to have two holidays so near together. The holidays are right enough, but it is the snip in the wages Which takes the gilt off the gingerbread.

The Mayoress of Warrington has commit- ted herself to .a graceful act in promising to provide a Jubilee medal for every child who takes part in the procession. As some eight or ten thousand mementoes will be needed, it will be seen that a considerable sum will be required. It will be pleasant. for the children to remember that the medals of the first lady in the land are the gift of the first lady in the town—for the time being.

Mr. Gladstone is not a rich man; but there was a disposition. in Tory quarters, to sneer when it was announced that he was contributing £5O towards the fund for the Imperial Institute. These ill-natured people were in too great a hurry; the People's William hail not exhausted his generosity; he is giving Lso towards a treat for the aged poor of Hawarden; and Zzoo to the Church House scheme. They will perhaps have a ,good word to say, now that he contributes ~ctuffing to that fat goose—the Church.

Referring to the dividends from breweries, and contributions therefrom for "building cathedrals and so on," Mr. Spurgeon says— " he should think it would want a great deal of passing through the fire and through the water before such leprous and defiling gold •could be laid upon the altar of God." We commend this frank expression of opinion to certain of the clergy of Warrington ; they ought to be able just now to point the moral. "Punch" has a pleasant greeting for the Emperor William on his ninetieth birthday. The following is the last of several good verses on the occasion : " rOl4 old, Father 'William?" cried Pun. "Time has twirled His eass half in vain, /should say, Let me wish you at least—on behalf of the World— Many Happy Returns of the Dar!"

Dr. Pankhurst has rendered a public ser- vice as well as vindicated his own dsaarac- fel by taking proceedings against Colonel Hamilton, for libelling him with regasd to his religious views. The £6O damages car- ries costs, of course; and the member for Rotherhithe will therefore be made to feel that he cannot with impunity impute atheis- tical nonsense to a political opponent.

Mrs, Werelen, of Bank Quay, Warrington, has given birth to triplets. The little things soon succumbed in the struggle for existence they died next day. it is stated that the triplets bring the number up to five in about twelve months. Fortunately the husband is a nurnber-taker on the railway; it requires a nunaber-taker under such circumstances to keep count. The law of compensation holds good here and everywhere.

An Earlestown anti-vaccinator who has been subjected to a fine for breach of the law has been subjected, too, to police pre- parations for a distraint, notwithstandino the fact that the fine had been paid. CLERKSHIP TO RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—The office of clerk to Runcorn School Board is vacant through the resignation of Mr F Rigby, and the Board invite applica- time for the position before Thareday next. EVANGELISTIC SERVICES AT WIDNES.—The evangelistic mission services which have been conducted in Hutchinson- street Primitive Methodist Chapel during the past fortnight were brought to a close on Thursday. The ministrations of Mr. T. Marshall, of Southport, who has acted as leader was Very successful. LACEY•STREBT WESLEYAN SCHOOL, WIDNES.—The an- nual gathering for the distribution of prizes to the children' attending this school took place on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. B. Brown. About 150 scholars re- ceived medals or books at the bands of Mr. Burden and Mrs. Bryant for their labours in connection with the Mis- sionary Society. PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.-011 Tuesday evening Miss Evans, daughter of Mr. Jonah Evans, general manager, of the Runcorn Co-operative Society, was presented with a handsome timepiece on the occasion, of her marriage to Mr. Owen Thomas. The presentation was made at the Welsh Chapel, in Rutland-street, where Miss Evans bad officiate I as organist for a number of years. Et-Lc-mon or GUARDIANS AT RIINcooN.—To-dav is th a last day for receiving nominations of guardians to the Run- corn Union. The five retiring members for Runcorn town- ship are Messrs. W. Whittaker, S. Taylor, P. Speakman, W. Fisher, and W. Farrell. Mr. Whittaker, who has long and faithfully represented Runcorn, doss not seek re-election. Very little interest is taken in the event, and it has not transpired who is nominated to fill the vacancy. We understand that at Weston Mr. R. Clarke intends to oppose the sitting guardian, Mr. E. Aaron. BRUNSWICK IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN —Mr. Jas. Patin Contributed a critical essay on '6 Macbeth " to the above society, on Wednesday evening. He examined, Ist the moral position of Macbeth before his first great crime, 2nd, the steps and temptations by which he was led to con- template and commit it.; 3rd, the succeeding crimes; and 4th, the final and permanent changes wrought in Macbeth's character by the whole course of events in the play. The essayist was congratulated by each succeeding speaker on the success with which he had interpreted Shakespeare's evident intention in the construction of the play. Wipritus GYMNASIUM HARR:Mos.—Eight members of the Widnes Gymnasium Harriers enjoyed a good spin last Saturday. The course taken was through Appleton and Cronton to Rainbill. The roads mid fields were in a fair condition for travelling. The pace from Rainhill home was very fast, but the members kept well together until Fern- worth was reached, when the rate of going was considered too warm for the majority of the runners, and they gradu- ally stopped. P. McMahon and Dick Evans, however, still raced ahead, and got home firet by 500 or 600 yards. Etheridge, 'Kearns, and Boscow were the next as-

;teals. RIIIICORY BOARD OF Commisstoxeas.—A special meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. P. Speakman presided, and there were present Messrs. Dobson, Grine Hankinson, Mel- , ior, Farrell, end Marshall (secretary.)—dn the recommenda- tion of the General Purposes Committee Messrs. Handley and Beall account of £ll 10e 9d, for re-hanging the fire- ' bell and otherwise putting it in efficient working order, was passed; as was also an account of £34 8s 7d from Messrs. ' Brundrit and Co., being the Cost of the palisading enclosing the nightsoil tipping wharf in Mill-street, recommended by the Health Committee. Accounts amounting to £3OO 15e 10d were also passed to close the financial year, and it I was resolved that irrecoverable arrears of rates amounting to £lOl 13s 9d be allowed.--The Chairman congratulated the members on the cleat' of a successful year, remariting that the finances were in a very satisfactory state. Waotas Loom BOARD BLECTION.—The ratepayers will no doubt be glad to learn that the expense of a contested , elected has been avoided, and the five retiring members— , mann i 'll Gossage, 32., 11 Gaskell, jun., E Carey, T Handley, and S Sadler—retain their seats. These gentlemen are the nominees of the Owners and Occupiers' Association, land haviag served the ratepayers ably and conscientiously ifor a considerable number of years, it was generally felt I their re-election was sure. The Rev George Bend. vicar of earnworth, asked the association to only nominate four candidates, and allow the fifth place to be filled by a person ,of his:choice. Upon the association declining this overture, oven under the threat of a contest, the reverend gentleman and Mr J Hargreaves, licensed victualler, and Mr Georged INeil, pawnbroker, Widnes-road, were nominated; the two latter by Mr Bond. On Thursday afternoon, however, the three gentlemen retired, and no contest will therefore take place. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY.—A meeting of the Widnes , Free Library Committee was held on Taursday afternoon. Mr li Wade Deacon presided, and there word present—Dr O'Reeffe, Messrs S Robinson, S Sadler. E Carey, J Morri- son. B Brows. and J T Allen (clerk to the Local Board). Mr T Laurie, of London, whose „contract for the snooty of books had been accepted, wrote stating that en the parcels of hooks he had already forwarded Ise would lose from £l5 to MO, aid he declined to proceed with the contract.—The Chairman remarked that he had had an interview with Mr Laurie in London. and the long and short of it was that that gentleman had taken the coot:ant too cheap, and had now backed out of his bargatin.—After some conversation it WAS deoided that Mr J Hough, of Widnes, should complete the contract at an allowance of 30 per cent.—The Clerk said Miss Proctor, the librarian, had supplied him with the following f.gures of the attendance at the reading 'room : On Saturday there were $BB vieitore, Monday 580, Tuesdey 555, Wednesday 051.—in answer to Mr Robinson, the Chairmen said there was no limit as to the age of persons admitted.—Mr Morrieon said on the previous day the room was half filled with boys who ought to be at school—The Chairman. There is nothing,* simpler than to send an at- tendance officer. If he could catch all the runaways in the Library he would have a fine time of it.—Dr O'Keeffe said the novelty of the affair would wear off in time.—The Chairman said if it went on like this there would not be sufficient room for adults.—Mr Morrison remarked that there was a great many boys attended the St. Helens read- ing room, and they would have to provide a aritible room for them like they slid in that town.—Mr Sadler said he should be sorry to see boys excluded on any consideration. —'the Chairman considered the wisest course at the present time WAS to allow Miss Proctor to net her own discretion in the management of the room, and make rules when they had had experience.—The Chairman was empowered to carry out certain improvements needed for the room,

, A MAN'S THUMB BIT OFF BY A 'BORST.—A. carter named 'Knowles, of. Hough Green, was, on Thursday, afternoon, backing a 'horse yoked to a luny, belonging to the Mancheater, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Com- pany, when 'the animal snapped his hand, and completely bit the end of his thumb off. He was attended by Mr. Lane, assistant to Dr. O'Neil. . .

MR. LUKE FILDES. -- The " Architect " says "south Kensington will of course take some credit for the success of the new Academician, Mr. Fildes, who was at oae time a student in training. But in those days, we believe, it was supposed that he was best fitted to be a decorative artist." EXTRAORD/NARY DISCOVERY /N CHESHIRE.— The body of a female child with two heads, two spines, and an unnatural number of limbs was found on Friday in a brickfleld at Acton Vale, Ac- ton. The police believe that it has been in a mu- seum or ashibition, it seeming to have been im- Mersed in spirits. • SWINE FEVER.—On Monday evening the Clerk of the Peace for Lancashire was informed that swine fever had appeared on the premises of John Wil- liams, Garston, and James Blackburn, Yew Tree Farm, Culcheth. In the former case four animals had been killed and two had died, and in the latter one had been killed and two had died. A Nzwyort Morn IN Tuounix.—A deaf and dumb man named John Pickavaace was charged on Mon- day, at the Warrington Occasional Court-house, Horsemarket-street, with doing wilful damage to a window at the Wellington Hotel, Newton. The damage was assessed at over £2, and the excuse ' offered by - the prisoner was that he was drunk when he broke the window. In default of paying a fine of 5s and costs, and a considerably reduced sum for the damage done, he was committed to prison for fourteen days. Rim= AsYrnm.—At the adjourned annual session of county magistrates, to be held on the 31st inst., the notices of motion comprise one to the effect that a sum not exceeding £17,000 be raised, under the provisions of the Lunatic Asylums Act, 1853, and expended under the direction of the Committee of Visitors for the completion of the new annexe of Rainhill Asylum, and that the General Finanee Committee be authorised, if they think fit, to borrow the whole or any part of that sum on mortgage of the county rates. Tan 110"zem VISIT TO MANCHESTER.—The follow- ing appears in " Truth " :—On the occasion of their visit to Manchester the Prince and Princess of Wales are to stay at Tatton Park with Lord and Lady Egerton, and not in the city as had been pro- ' posed by the Corporation. They will arrive at linutsford on the evening of Monday, May 2. The next day will be devoted to the Manchester cere- mony, and, in the afternoon of Wednesday, the 4th, their Royal Highnesses will return to London from Manchester, where they are to pass the morning. Ttitt Princess Louise of Wales is expected to accom-

pany her parents. "Civil. SERVICE Aurrincenc."—This is the title Of a new work compiled by Mr. J. Keefe, F.R.G.S., of Liverpool and Manchester. It consists of numer- ous examination papers set in recent years to can- didates fcer men, boy, and female clerkships, excise, customs, &c., together with answers to all the pro- blems. Among recent papers included in this com- pendium of arithrnedc are those set at the excise and customs competitions in 1886, and the paper set for the January customs (1887) examination. Not the least valuable feature of the book is the ap- pendix, which contains ample instruction on the chief difficulties of advanced arithmetic. MR. SPURGEON AND THE BREWERY QUESTION. —Speaking on Tuesday night at the fifth anniver- sary of the Metropolitan Tabernacle Blue Ribbon Total Abstinence Society, Mr. Spurgeon said that he would like to hear from Mr. Palmer or Mr. Noble (who occupied seats on the platform) an explana- tion of one thing, viz: What was the reason of these limited liability companies for' the transfer- ence of breweries, distilleries, and such like? Was it a bad sign, or was it a good sign? Was it that the gentlemen who had made a good deal of money in them wanted to save what they had got? He was not an old band at understanding these mys- teries. He heard that several clergymen had ap- plied for shares in these breweries. (A voice: "Shame.") What- that friend over there said, he thought too. He wondered what Christian people did with the dividends from these companies. What did they wash the money in before they took it? and if they contributed it to the cause of God, building cathedrals, and so on, what did they do be- fore they presented it to God? He should think it would want a great deal of passing through the fire and through the water before such leprws and defiling gold could be laid upon the altar or God. MR. J. MORLEY AND Mn. BROADHURST ON FREE LlBRARlES.—AriVinsford, it has been decided to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee by the erection of a free library. Mr. J. H. Cooke, solicitor, and hon. secretary of the movement, has received letters on the subject from the Right lion. John Morley, M.P., and Mr. Henry Broadhurst, secretary to the Trades' Union Congress. Mr. Morley says;—" The immense popularity and undoubted usefulness of a free library have been amply proved in every place where the experience has been tried. There can be no greater encouragement to new experiments than the past success of this excellent movement." Mr. Broadhurat says :—"Next to elementally edam- 1 tion, the ratepayers can scarcely invest their money in more profitable or more desirable a, manner than in a free library. By means of these institutions written knowledge is brought within reach of the poorest. Up to the present it has only been in the power 04 the rich and well-to-do to provide them- selves with the best works for the formation of the character and the instruction of the mind. Theonly superiority that one man has over another is in knowledge and character. Free libraries are there• - fore a direct aid to the promotion of equality among men. I hope that the working classes of the district will heartily support your under- taking." • ALLEGED THEFTS BY A WARRINGTONIAN AT Wm-Ms.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Thomas Long- shaw, labourer, of Lloyd-street, Warrington, was charged with having, 'between the 10th and 15th inst., stolen from Mr. Edward Percy, contractor, of Sutton's-lane, Widnes, seven sacks, a coat, and two spades, value altogether 28s. Prisoner, it appeared, had been in Percy's employ, and had availed him- self of that opportunity to "annex" the goods mentioned in the charge. They had been missed at various times between the dates mentioned, The sacks prisoner sold to Mrs. Simcock, wife of Mr. F. T. Simcock, marine store dealer, Appleton-street, for 9d, stating that he was a nightsoil man, and had found them in the ashpit ; and one of the spades and the coat he also sold to Mrs. Simcock for is and 3d respectively. The other spade he sold to a forge- man named Thomas Jones, of Philip-street, War- rington, giving as his excuse for wanting to get rid of it that the job he had been working at was fin- ished. He added that he had given 3s 6d for it. Ultimately a bargain Was struck that .Tones should buy it for Is, the prisoner to pay for a pint of beer. Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions. There was a further charge against Longshaw of stealing from the Mill- field Inn, Millfiald-road, Widnes, a bottle of whis- key, value 38 6d. the property of Mr. Thomas Lee, the landlord, but it was withdrawn. THE PARKHURST SLANDER CASE.—Considerable interest was excited by the hearing of the case, Pankhurst v. Hamilton, in the Queen's Bench Divi-i, sion, before Mr. Justice Grove and a special jury. The plaintiff, Dr. Pankhurst, is a barrister, of Man- chester, and of the Northern Circuit, and the defen- dant, Colonel Hamilton, who also hails from Man- , chester, is a son-in-law of Colonel George McCorquo- dale, J.P., Newton-le-Willows; a colonel of volun- teem, a director of the well-known printing firm of MeCorquodale and Co., printers, and a member of Parliament in the Conservative interest for the Rotherhithe division of the borough of Southwark. The plaintiff claimed £lO,OOO for the publication of a libel charging him with having publicly denied the existence of a God, and with saying "If there is a God I defy God," and also "if there is a devil I am in a position to defy the devil." The alleged slander was spoken of at a meeting of elec- tors, and the libel was printed in various forms and distributed throughout the constituency. The publication was substantially admitted, and the defence was that it was published bona fide in the full belief that. it was true and privilege was claimed. The case occupied several days in hear- ing.—During the hearing on Monday a scene was I caused in the court by the defendant, Colonel Ham- ilton, stating that he was informed by Sir Charles Russell, who was conducting the case for Dr. Pank- hurst, that the plaintiff entertained atheistical views. Sir Charles indignantly denied this, and asked to be put in the witness-box, but lunch inter- vening, and the Solicitor-General throwing oil on the troubled waters, the defendant withdrew the statement, and the matter ended.—On Tuesday counsel addressed the jury on each side, and prior to the judge's summing up the jury said they were agreed as to their verdict, but wished to retire to consider the damages.—The jury returned into court with a verdict for the plaintiff, awarding him 40s damages for the slander, and £6O damages for the libel, with Costs.

THE ALTRINCKAM JIIBELEE MOVEMENT. The committee having the direction of this movement ,is carrying it forward vigorously. It is proposed to celebrate the Jubilee by raising a sum to convert the Literary Institution into a free library and news-room for the use of the inhabitants of Al- trincham, Bowdon, Dunham Massey. Hale. and Tim- perley. . PENKETH WESLEYA.N SCHOOLS.—An advertise- ment in another column states that a bazaar, in aid of the enlargement of the day and Sunday schools, at Penketh, will be held in the Wesleyan School- room, Bold-street, Warrington, on Wednesday and Thursday next. The Mayor will, it is expectect open the bazaar on Wednesday'. The exist- ing Wesleyan School premises at Penketh have for a long time been found inadequate for the requirements of the neighbourhood, and consequently it was determined to increase the ac- commodation. The estimated cost of the enlarge- ment proposed is about .£9OO, towards which about .E5OO has been promised, leaving £4OO to be raised. It is hoped that the bazaar to be held will result in a good sum' being raised, as every possible effort has been made to render it a success.

TIM LATE LORD GERAYLD.—" Truth" says Lord Gerard was one of the most popular men in Lancashire. He possessed an .immense fortune, his estates being extensive and very valuable, and everything that he undertook was done en prince. His charities of every description were munificent. The splendour of his Shrievalty in 1859 is still re- membered in the county, and his hospitalities at Garswood. his place near Warrington, were most brilliant. Lord Gerard was one of the oldest and most distinguished Catholic families. One of his ancestors, who rendered great services to Mary Queen of Scots, was created a baronet on the first day the Order was instituted,and James I. gave him back the .£4,000 he had paid for the dignity. The ancient Lancashire seat of the Gerarde, Bryn Hall, is in ruins.

div.head: MR. W. LI JUDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MR. W. LI JUDE AT RUNCORN.

_ Mr. W. H. Jude, principal of the Liverpool College School, en Monday evening delivered a lecture on a Toe power of music" in Hui corn Public Hall. The eminent musician appealed in tie interest of the Young Men's Christian associatimn, and the president of that institute, Mr J,40101 Pritchard, occupied the chair. Although the audi- ence wet' not of huge proportions, local musical taste and Culture was well represented, and it is gratifying to know that the funds of the Association will be considerably aug- tanned as a result. In itself interesting and instructive, the lecture, however, was evidently intended merely as en in- troduction to the performance of instrumental and vocal music, illustrative of various styles and harmony, and for this purpose was admirably conceived and delivered. The power of music in exciting military ardour, and its very antithesis, religious fervour, and the pleasure and happiness it contributed to the social circle, was eloquently commen- ted upon. As to our Church music, Mr. Jade was far from complimentary. He made some scathing observations upon the narrow mindedness of those who hid control of the ser- vices, and said it teas a shame and a standing disgrace to those in power who had allowed the greater portion of Mozart's and Heydn's masses to be ruthlessly bundled out of their churches. The Church of England had amongst her greatest inheritance the rich legacy of Henry Purcell, one of the most extraordinary geniuses this or any other country could, boast of. Out of the hundreds of sublime anthems he had written, about five were allowed to be beard in our Cathedral Churches; and this he thought from an ardent desire on the part of the authorities to curtail in every possiole way any extended efforts made from time to time to beautify and adorn a liturgy in itself full of pathos and power, and from a literary and artistic point of view, per- haps perfection. Mr. Jude spoke of the outpour- ings of the Salvation Army as degraded awl debas- ing. A brief, review of the compositions of Bach and Handel was followed by the lecturer playing on the piano a fugue in D major of the former's, and "The harmonious black. smith" of the latter; and then dealing with vocal music, he said none could surpass the ballad writers of our own coun- try. He sang with much pathos and power that much neg- lected but sweet ballad cf Samuel Lover. "What will you do, love;" and he raised the audience to a high pitch of enthusiasm a brief space later by his dramatic rendering of the descriptive scene, "The ship on fire," by Henry Russell. After expressing tbe wish that some one would do for our miners what Dibdin had done for our sailors, Mr. Jude gave his own descriptive.ballad, "Deep in the mine," which 11118 listened to with rapt attention, and loudly applauded. He also performed on the piano compositions by Beethoven, , Mendelstiohn, Conpein, and .Rockstro„ and concluded an elevating and ennobling musical entertainment by playing : on the harmonium a fantasia on Irish and Scotch airs, writ- ten by himself, in which he produced some extraordinary . effects. He was compelled to respond to the vociferous ap- ; platise awarded him for his efforts, and he was heartily , thanked on the motion of Mr. J. Johnson, seconded by Mr F. Burman.

The interest on the money was at the pretty high rate of five per cent., and compelled them to raise £5O to meet that solitary obligation. (Hear, hear.) The congiegation worshipping in Green- way-road Chapel, he was informed, had its nucleus formed some fifty years ago in a little lowly cottage at the top of Nelson-street. The three or four earnest men who banded themselves together to form a church came from Preston Brook direction, and be understood that Preston Brook still held superiority by being called the centre of the circuit. (Hear. hear.) The congregation from Nelson-street came te the building in which they were that day assembled, and which performed the double duty of school and chapel. From there the congregation migrated to the chapel in Greenway-road, which was built at a cost of .41,630 The organ cost £3OO. and the new heating appa- ratus and connections cost .£9O, making the total amount .£2,020.
