a CORY RULES. DALLAM BREWERY F.C. T. BEWSEY ROVERS F.C.—This game ended in a victory for the Brewery by 2 goals, 2 tries, and 3 minors to nil. FRODSRLM V. HALTON.—Plived at Frorlsham on Satur- day. The game was rather one-sided, the borne team being better, both forwards and behind. The home backs played a splendid passing game, which finally brought the follow- ing result :—Frodaham, two goals, five tries, eight minors. to Halton nil. Darliagton dropped a splendid goal, the tries were got as follows: Mercer two, Darlington one. Owen one, Ashworth one, and Thomas one. Rogers and Webb played a capital back game, having repeatedly hard lines in not scoring. SANHEY V. SALE (A TEAM3).—Thi3 match was played at Sankey on Saturday, and after a pleas tot game of two thirties resulted in a win for Sankey. Sankey won the toss and elected be play down hill. Sale kicked off, and Jeffer- son returned into touch, and Sankey rushed the ball down the field to half way. Jeff-rsoo passed to Barton. and this player ran into the Sale taenty-five, and passed to Walley who mulled the pass. From a scrimmage Jefferson ran to within a yard off the line. From anetherscrimage Sale touelakd down. At half time scores were, Sankey one minor, Sa e nil. After change of ends Sankey kicked off, and no return being made, Highley, Dykes, and Bird dribbled to the Sale twenty-five. Barton here intercepted a pass, and scored wkat seemed to be a fair try, but the referee ruled otherwise. Blackledge next scored a fine try, Barton failing at the goal. After the drop out Sankey still ;neared, some fine passing bringing them to the Sale line,*and they dribbled the ball over the line, but it went into touch is goal. The game ended with Sankey the winners by one try and two minors to Sale nil. Barton ran and kicked in fine style. Jefferson and Blackledge passed well, and the forwards played well to a man. Sankey were poorly represented. RUNCORN 2tan Traaat Y. LITHICRLAND.—Tbese teams met on Sa urday. on the ground of the former. A good game I was the result, Runcorn winning by one god and eight minor points to Litherland one try and one minor. Runcorn only played fourteen men, the captain having to leave the field 30011 after starting. The home team kicked eff, and the ball was well returned. Freeman, obtaining, put in a nice run to the borne line, wben, from a scrimmage, Larkin scrambled over and grounded the ball, the kick at goal failing. Brazendale dropped out, and Abrams, Whitby, Hine ick, and GiVens following well up took play to the visitors' line, when Abrams dribbled over, but lost posses- sion, and Freeman saved. Whitby replied to the drop out, and sent the oval close to the line. Play then tecarne very exciting, and Whitby getting hold crossed the line, but in grounding lost the ball, and Freeman ran it out. Half- time was soon afterwards called, leaving the score—Lither- land, one try and one minor to Runcorn two minors. On re-etarting, loose play ensued, and the borne team, having all the beet of the day, kept the ball continually in their Opponents' quarters, and had very hard line, on several occasions is not scoring. Abrams' Riley, and Whitby took the bail over the line, but were unfertunate in grounding on each eccasidn. As time was drawing to a close play be- came exceedingly fast and exciting, and Clare getting hold made a splendid attempt at goal, the ball striking the post and rebounding into the field of play again. From a scrim- mage, the ball coming loose. Clare obtained possession, and transferred to Riley, who (after several splendid attempts to get over) crossed the line and gained a meritorious try close to touch, amidst vociferous cheering, which was renewed when Brazendale piloted, the ball over the bar with a splendid kick. No side Was afterwards called, and a mast stubbornly and well-contested game ended as above. WARRINGTON 2:3D TRAM V. WARRINGTON RANGERS ler. —This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. BncklPv wen the toss and Whittle kicked off against the wind, Evans returning, and play resting in the centre. Some exciting play took place during the first half, and at the call of half-time the score stood Warrington 1 try and 1 minor, to Rangers 1 minor Savage restarted the game, Myles returning in touch. Bate. Warburton. and Thornley brake away and dribbled over the line. Edwards attains by kicking dead. From the drop oat Holmes, Howarth, and Teare ran the ball to the line, but Mokell relieved to vat- ter flag, and Mather getting hold almost got in, Edwards shortly afterwards kicking dead. Bihby returned the drop out, and Evans was collared before he could part with the leather. Minshall, Buckley, and Sanders removed the pressure by a good dribble to centre. where Sanson passed to Evans, who made a grand run, being brought down by Whittle. Tbornley, Coyne, and Bibby went. away-with a dribble, but Sullen WWI. On the ball be coming loose from the scrimmage, Maskell kicked to Brown, who made a splendid return, and Edwards mulling, Bate kicked over the line and gained a good try. Boardman failed at the place. From the drop out the ball went into touch, and Thornley obtaining possession from the line out was instrumental in taking play to the line, a minor result- ing. Myles returned the drop out, and Mather collared Maßkell before he could get away. Barlow, &MAU% and Buckley removed play to centre by a nice dribble, but Myles saved in fine style. Boardman here changed places with Randlee. From a scrimmage in the centre Whittl, transferred to Boardman, who pot in a good run and kink, and Myles rushing up dribbled to the line, Bate gaining a try. The attempt at goal by Howarth was unsuccessful. Shortly after the drop out Whittle again passed to Board- man, who kicked dawn tke field, and following well up obtained a grand try, Howarth failing at place. Warring- ton eventually won by four tries and three minors to Ran- gers one minor. Teams :—Warrington End Team: Brown full back; Randle, Mather, Myles, three-quarter backs; Boardman and Whittle, half-backs; Howarth, Thornley, Tears, Bibby. Warburton, Bate, Holmes, Coyne, and Coyne, forwards. Ranger,: Edwards. fall back; Evans, SIII3OII, and Masten, three-quarter backs; Cook and Bellis, half- backs ; Buckley, Sanders. Barlow, Savage, Hill, Smith, Hastings, Clough, and Minshall, forwards. Referee, Mr. T. Pemberton. • Sara v. Rtruconw.—This match was played on Saturday afternoon at Sale. Lings kicked off for the home team, and W. Hughes returned, and loose play ensued in Sale quar- ters. Cowell' got hold and rushed across the field, but went into touch. From the lies out Riley got poesession and made a good run, but was brought down by Stephens when just beginning to look dangerous. Walters then passed to Cowell. who got in a good run and kick to centre, where scrirrmages ensued for some time. Andrews picked up and pissed to Riley. and he transferred to Davies, who made a good run, but lost the ball. Riley took up the movement, and was only collared on the goal line, when be passed to Davies, who got in near touch. Broady failed at the place. Hunt dropped out, and a (pick return being effected, scrimmages tool place on the Sale goal line. Stephens relieved well, and Davies retaliated, hut was well collared by Walters. The ball then travelled across the field, where Cawley got off, but was tackled by Cowsill. After a series of scrimmages in neutral ground the Sale for- wards dribbled the ball to the Rancorn ground headed by Rooker. Stephens picked up, but could not gat far, and Sale were forced back to centre, where Lewis picked up and ran in between the posts. Broady failed at an easy place. After the drop out the Sale line was at once placed in jeopardy, and Lewis again got In, no goal resulting. After the drop out a dead ball was registered to Sale after a smart piece of play by Rant Stephens kicking well, and the forwards following up, took play to the Runcorn lines, but the visi- tor's forwards quickly rushed the ball back to centre. At half-time the score was—Runcorn three tries to Silo one minor. After the change of ends loose play ensued, and Davies kicked a dead ball. Long kicks were then indulged in, and Faulkner getting hold passed to Wainwright, who gained a try, Broady taking the place, but failing. Sale forwards afterwards dribbled from one end of the field to the other, and almost scored a try, but a dead ball war, their only reward. Wainwright got hold, and ran and pieced to Cawley, ard he to Riley, who gained a try under the posts for Ralicorn. Lewis took the place, but no goal resulted. After some loose play a scrimmage was formed near-the Sale uprights. Walters relieved with a good run, and Cow- sill took the leather on. A pack was then formed opposite the Sale goal; a dead ball only resulted. Andrews then got in for Runcorn, Wood failing at goal, and just before the close Wainwright dropped a goal from a pass by Broady. At the call of time the score was—Kuncorn 1 goal, 6 tries, and 4 minors, to Sale 3 minors. The passing of the visi- tors was grand. Teams :—Runcorn : T. Woods, hack; Cawley, Riley, and T. Davies, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and rf. G. Andrewe, half-backs; Wright, Broady, W. Faulkner, Lewis, J. Clarke, J. Gatley, Barnes, Wain. wright, and W. Hughes, forwards. Sale: T. Babington, back' W. Stephens, C. Williams, and T. Comet], three- quarter backs; S. Broughton and A. Walters, half-backs • , W. Bunt *.Y. Hardy, P. R. Rooker. C. Chapman, W.' Jones, D. Wood, F. Newton, A. Armitage, and T. Lungs, forwards. RUNCORN V. Ma. A. W. Rio's Team —The latter gen- tlemanbrought a stroug comaination to Runcorn on Wednes- day, composed principally of prominent players from several Manchester clubs, Widnes also contribuling a quota, and Liverpool one in the person of A T Kemble. Play was 'somewhat in favour of the "mixed ones" daring the first period, but Runcorn completely defeated their opponents in the Second half, leaving the ground easy winners. To a good attendance Wright kicked off for Runcorn, and only a moderate response being at hand, a scrimmage was formed, but the Manchester team, by sure kicking arid tackling, soon invaded the houto quarters. and Morris made an ex- cellent drop at goal, but the ball striking the bar, Hardman was quickly on to it and grounded, but only an easy place failure followed. 3ryBeeMemolbgegeswourptahtlynehxatd mtoadte ou llebr,w isdman trk.,:icnd, the green j In succession. Notwithstanding the excellent running by Speakman. Davies, and H Hughes, the combination of their opponents still kept the play in the Runcorn quar- ters, and at bait time the home team had only scored a minor to one try and four minors. A W Read re.corn- meneed, and as there was only a feeble return, Runcorn were soon busy, and a powerful kick by Davies quickly brought a minor to the home team, who, having the wind, quickened np considerably, another minor quickly follow- ing. The home team then heat their opponents in the loose play ;"Wright dashed through, but losing the ball. Wain- wright completed the try, Broady landing another goal. Andrews secured from the kick off, and ran splendidly, another.bringing ta enboint a minor, a powerful kick quickly adding ble, Anderton, and Hardman then brought the ball to the Runcorn 25, but it did not long remain there, some excellent kicking by H Hughes and Broady quickly landing play within the mixed team's 25. Speakman then took a pass and kicked a grand goal, the ball striking the posts in its course. Another minor followed

to Bancorp, who were now overplaying their opponents at all points. Another effort soon landed the green jerseys at the line, and Speakman, after losing the ball, soon regained possession from a neat pass and just missed dropping another goal. There was no staying the home players, who were too quick for their opponeats. Wright soon secured, and dashing away was quickly over, Broady's effort striking the bar and rebounding into play. The home players now bad matters to their own hands, and Davies, after a grand dodgy run, planted betwixt the posts Broady easily scor- ing. Edge and Mothersill were indefatigable at this point in saving, but do what they would the excellent running and passing ef the wearers of the green corn- pletely nonplussed all efforts at defence, and ere long Speakman had crossed the line, but after a dispute a minor only was given, a similar decision following an excellent run by II Hughes, but the latter quickly added a try, the result of an excellent effort; Runcorn leaving the field easy winners by four goals, one try, and ten minors to one try and four minors. Teams—Runcorn: T Woods. beck; T Davies, H C Speakman. and H Cawley, three-quarter backs ; H Hualles and H Andrews, half backs ; W Broady, W Hughes, W Wright, W Faulkner, J Clarke, J Lewis, U Wainwright, T Barnes, and J Gatley, forwards. Mr Read's Team: Molesworth (Manchester), back; Mothersill (Manchester), Parkinson and Morris (Widnes), three-quarter backs; Edge (Broughton Rangers) and Hardy (Sale), half-backs ; A W Read, J W Clegg, Whitworth, and ALI Midwood kMan- chaster), AT Kemble (Liverpool), W 11,PLean (Broughton), C Anderton (Free Wanderers), Hughes, and Hardman (Wid- nes), forwards. WEST LANCASBIRE CUP COMPETITION. WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.

In the semi-final ties,i the above cup competition the Warrington and Wigan teams met on the neutral ground of the St. Helens Recreation Clu'e. Great interest was taken in the eveut, special trains being ran from Warrington, Wigan, and Widnes, and on the field there were over 8,004 spectators. The ground was in excellent condition, and gave every opportunity for a good contest. The spectators were apparently strung up to the highest pitch of enthus- iasm in the coarse of the game, and the cheers of the par-i tisane of the respective teams were loud and frequent. On a start being made, Frank Turner kicked off for Warrington, and soon after Mitchinson led through with a dribble into the aVarrington half. Antrobas stopped the rush, and Fair. Tureer, aided by Rigby and Littlewood, soon transferred the game to centre field. Mitchinson aeaio obtained possession, and put in a fine run and maimed the Warrington quarter flag before he was held. Here the ball fell into touch, and from a long throw in, Atkinson secured, and was within a yard of the Warrington lines, when he was brought down. Some vigorous play then took place, and Whittle managed to rush over the line and scored a try behind the posts amid great cheering. Ander- ton kicked from a position immediately in front of the goal, and landed a goal. Funk Turner set the ball in motion again, and Jolley followed up smartly, entered the Wigan half, but was brought down by Whittle. From a long pass by Hunter to Mitchinson the latter was splendidly collared by Barnes. Mitchinson led through with a dribble; and the Warrington lines were again invaded, and the second try was scored ; but the point was disallowed, and the ball was brought back to the half-way flag. By strong forward play Warrington rushed through to the Wigan quarters, but levln say.d by klckine into touch. Warrington new began to prete their opponents, and valuable work was done by Barnes and Speakman. For some moments Wigan had to withstand the pressure of a strong attack, and numerous pocked scrimmages were the order of the day. Slavin re- lieved by a strong run and reached mid-field, where he was tackled by Jolley, and further progress prevented. From the scrimmage Morris made a neat pass to Anderton, and he cleverly dodged all his opponents until Massey stopped him safely in the Warrington half. Anderton passed the leather to Hunter, who entered the Warrington quarters. Hunter finished by a long kick, which landed the ball dead over the line. Wigan continued their attack, and Hunter was again on the point of running over the line when Jolley pushed him into touch. From a line out Mitchinson made a wild pass, and the ball fell into the hands of Barnes, who drew forth tremendous cheers for a capital run to the Wigan quarter, where Slavin saved. Wigan improved their lost ground when Mitchinson led a forward dribble to the Wigan quarters, Appleton saving by kicking into touch. Barnes then got in a long kick, and .a return was made by Slevin, and the ball fell among the forwards at mid-field. The Warrington forwards led through with a strong rash, and by splendid play reached the quarters. From a kick Barnes secured, and from be- , hind the pack made a long punt. He followed up with smartness, and securing the ball got over the line. The Wigan men appealed for offside, but the referee gave his decision in favour of Warrington. Speakman made the attempt at goal, but did not succeed. Frank Turner kicked off for Warrington, and Wigan were soon placed on the defensive, the Warrington forwards showing up in capital form. From the scrimmage Seeakrnan passed to Barnes, who kicked over the line. Slevin secured possession, but was compelled to touch down. At this "point Jolley retired hurt. and Frank Turner was placed behind. When half-time was celled the Warrington men were close to the line of their opponents, the score etandieg—Wigan. nine points; Warrington, five Points. In n. sic )11 i elf Jolley returned to his place, Andorton took Slevin's place at full back, while Slavin was trans- ferred to the left wing three-quarter. Frank Turner kicked off for Warrington, and directly after Hunter secured a free ' kick. Some severe scrimmaging took place when sudden ly Barnes emerged with the ball at his feet, and entered the Mean half, where Anderton saved. Brayshaw led through with a splendid dribble, and the Wigan men then advanced to the Warrington line where an exciting scrimmmage took place, which lasted for more than five minutes Warrington contested every inch with great stubbornness, and be strong tackling and good combination in the rushes their lime of defence was absolutely invulner- able. Material relief was afforded when Frank Turner ob- tained a free kick for the charge of off side. From bis kick Ellison for Wigan secured a free kick in dangerous proxim- ity to the Warrington goal, but the kick by Anderson Niel. Appleton approached the ball horn behind his line, into the quarters, and Barnes following up with a splendid run placed the game in Wigan quarters, Shortly afterwards Morris was carried off the field owing to an injury to his face. On the resumption of play Littlewood and Rigby rushed through the Wigan line with the ball at their feet, and Samuels was compelled to concede a dead ball. The Wigan men, on the ball being brought out, rushed through into the Warrington half, where between them, Massey and Appleton mulled the ball. The Wigan men followed up, but their charge was stopped by Barnes. Packed scrimmages, in which Warrington had a decided advantage, left the game in the Warrington half until Mitchinson obtained some relief by a hee kick. Barnes returned, and the Wigan half was again fought. At this point, Morris having re- covered from his injury, re-entered the field. The game was then only notable for some minutes for its packed scrimmages in mid-field. From the pack Wigan rushed the opposing lines and forced a maul in goal, which resul- ted in a minor being scored by Wigan. Fair Turner brought out for Warrington, and Wigan again gave the Warrington men an anxious minute, as within two minutes they scored another dead ball. Warrington played a strong defensive game, but failed to prevent another minor being scored, and at call of time the result was a victory for Wigan by 12 points to 6. Teams :—Warrington : Appleton, full back; Jolley, Barnes, and Massey, three-quarters; Speakman and Antro- bus, half backs; Ashton (captain), Fairfield Turner, Frank Earner, Povey, Davies, Littlewood, Hayes, Hough, and Rigby, forwards. Wigan: Slavin, fall back; Anderton, Samuels and Hunter, three-quarter backs; Mitchinson and Morris, half backs; Brayshay, Whittle, Lowe, Kay, Atkin- son, Wardle, Dempsey, Booth, and Ellison, forwards. Um- pires: Mr. Trevor Smith and Mr. G. Vickers. Referee: Mr. A. T. Kemble, Liverpool.
ASSOCIATION RULES.
WIGAN ASSOCIATION CUP.-FINAL TIE.
EARLESTOWN V. IILYDOCK.

The final tie in the competition for the Wigan and Dip , trict Football Association Challenge Cop was played on the ground of the Wigan Football Club at Foolstock, on Satur- day afternoon, the competing teams being Earlestown and Haydock. Since the introduction of association foothill in the district the greatest rivalry has existed between the Earlestown and Havdock teams, and it has appeared to in- crease with advancing years. Or.?inary contests between the elevens has been productive of great excitement, owing to the recognised superiority of both over every other club in the neighbourhood, but when the teams have ben drawn together in cup ties the feeling of the respective supporters has increased ten-fold. Saturday was the second occasion upon which the teams have played in a cup contest, and a somewhat singular coincidence was that on the former oc- casion it was the final tie of the competition for the Wel- lington Challenge Cep, and Earleatown won by 2 goals to none. A few weeks ago the two clubs played a friendly match en the Haydock ground, and the home team deci- sively beat Earlestown by no less than four goals to one. Since then the anticipated meeting of the two elevens in the Wigan cup ties was eagerly awaited, and the battle of the champions for the honour of holding the Wigan and Dis- trict trophy, on Saturday last, raised the excitement to an intense pitch. The match took place on the ground at Poolotock, Wigan, and the rival teams were welcomed by large numbers of their supporters. who had come by train or waggonettes from Earlestown, Haydock, Ashton, Golborne, ato. There were several thousand spectators, and from the prolonged cheers which greeted the Haydock representa- tives, it was evident that they were the favourites of the day. Throughout the match play was of a most exciting character. Neither team had the advantage for sometime, but after the lapse of twenty minutes W. Shaw scared for Earlestonm amid great enthusiasm. This was the only point during the first half. In the second half a desperate struggle fir supremacy was witnessed, but Earles- town possessed a slight advantage all through and ultimately won by three goals to one. On the cessation of play the supporters of the Earlestown team evinced their delight by rushing on the field and en- thusiastically cheering their team. The players were raised shoulder high, and carried amid loud cheers outside the field. The result was about a true index of the state of the play. The winning team, to a man, played exceedingly well, and displayed an almost perfect combination, while their opponents did not display quite as much brilliancy in that respect. Hatton, of Haydock, wae the best player on the , field, his strong and accurate kicking being a feature of the match. The other players of the team failed to come up to the expectations of their supporters, and the latter were considerably disappointed at the result of the contest. The cep was afterwards presented to the winning team at the Railway Hotel, Wigan.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The hitherto victorious career of the Wa.rrington team in connection with the West Lancashire Cap was brought to an abrupt end on Saturday. The general impression had been that after disposing of Widnes nothing would prevent their appearance in the final tie, but in football, as in other things, the unexpected happens, and so Warrington have now to yield up the cap to the winner of to-day's. match between Avail and Wigan The play of the Warrington forwards was rather disappointing. They seemed disor- ganised, and lacked the spirit and dash which are generally conspicuous in their play. Neither did the backs play so well as is their wont, with the exception of Barnes, who has been highly complimented on hie display. Jolley, it should also be said, showed a good deal of his old form until hurt.
We bear that Ashton has invited hie team to accompany him to Liverpool to-day, to see the final. This is no doubt to take notes, and to see it possible where the mistake was made last week.

The Warrington Football Club, we understand, with a view to encouraging the junior clubs in the district, propose instituting a Local Junior Competition. Suitable medals will be given to the winners and runners up, and the con- tests will take place in the evenings during next month. The Warrington secretary desires that secretaries of clubs willing to compete will communicate with him at once.

We understand that Mr. Warren, the secretary of the Warrington Football Club has had numerous applications from clubs to play on the Warrington ground next week. Amongst those who have applied are St. Helens, Hall Southcoates' Free Wanderers, Southport Olympic, Cromp- ton, and Walton. The two semi-final ties in the West Lancashire Cup com- petition were brought off on Saturday with the following results :—Wigan beat Warrhgton on the ground of the St. Helens Recreation Club, by 12 points to 6; Aspull beat Tyldesley, at Wigan, by 6 points to 3. At a meeting of the West Lancashire Rugby Union Committee held at the Goal Hotel, Liverpool, on Saturday, it was decided that the final tie in the competition between Wigan and Aspull should take place to-day (Saturday) on the Liverpool ' Athletic Ground, Fairfield. The fourth round of ties in the Yorkshire Cup competi- tion were played In fine weather on Saturday. Batley v. Wakefield Trinity : About 15.000 persons witnessed this tie at Batley. The home team kicked off. Folios from a fair catch caused Batley to save. Ash then nearly ran in for the visitors, Pnd directly after he nearly dropped a goal, the ball striking one of the posts and rebounding. Falba, from a free kick for off-side tackling, sent the leather over the bar, but the point could not of course be scored. In the second half each side scored a touchdown. At the expira- tion of 80 minutes' play the result was a draws. Twenty minutes extra were played, but without any result, the match being drawn. Score: Wakefield. three minors ; Batley, one minor.—Leeds Parish Church v. Leeds St. John's : Played on former's ground before an immense crowd. In the first half Northend, making a mistake, let in M'Mullan, who got an easy try, and Potter kicked is goal. Lumley afterwards scored for the Parish, but Riley's kick failed. Nothing important was scored in the second half, St. John's winning by one goal and three minors to one try and two miners.—Liversedge v. Kirkstall : At Liversedge. Fisher did some splendid kicking, and from a pass by H. Barker dropped a goal for Liyersedge in the first half. On crossing over he ran in twice and placed a goal. -Ellis then got a try for Kirkstall. Score : Liversedge, two goals, one try, and one minor; Kirkstall, one try and one minor.— Stanningham v. Ossett : At Ossett. Manninghain got a bye through Bradford's disqualification. Ossett won by five miners to twe.

Under association rules the representative teams of Eng- land and Scotland met at Blackburn, on Saturday. The game was very closely contested, but ended in a win for Scotland by three goala to two. Scotland has now won ten !notifies, loot two, and drawn four.

SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC IN ELACKELIRN.—A virulent epi- demic of small-pox has broken Out in Blackburn, and the disease seems to be spreading with great rapidity, for in the course of the week over a dozen cases have been discovered and the unfortunate people removed to the Small-pox Hospital. All the sufferers are supposed to have caught it through some members of the theatrical professicn bringing it into the town.

SETEfifi GALE.—The strong westerly gale which prevailed on Wedneqday blew down a high wall forming part of the ruins of a burnt-out mill at Loughborough. A man named Adcock was crushed to death by the falling brickwork, and another man sustained injuries which raay prove fatal. At Plymouth the Greenock brigantine Kate was driven ashore, and a similar casualty happened to a schooner near Rams- gate. Both crews were rescued by lifeboats. A. NEWSPAPER PARAGRAPH. AND HOW IT SIVED A GENERAL'S MIL

The following statement, made by a well-known General besidos the unusual matter of value which it contains, will be Mend most readable and interesting : " MESsELS. EDITORS,—I have always believed most firm y in the Brotherhood of Men, and think every human being is in duty-bound to assist his fellow-man to the fullest extent of his power. The relation, therefore, id my personal ex- perience will, I trust, prove of benefit to many thousands in this country and India.

"For thirty-six years previous SO 1875 I had been a resi- dent of India. ?tiring this period the performance of my duties frequently exposed me, for months at a time, to the malarioue and poisonous emanations of the jungle, and ths fevers and diseases incident to a hot, moist climate. These repeated exposures finally resulted in a chronic disorder of the kidneys and liver, so common to the inhabitants of that country. This was some twelve years ago, when I finally became so seriously ill that I was obliged to return to Eag- laud. Upon my arrival I took to my bed, enduring untold agonies. My medical attendant Was puzzled as to the na- ture of my ailment until I commenced to pass small stones. From this I secured temporary relief, but relapsed from time to time, having the most distressing spells of sickness ima- ginable, with high-colmred water, fickle appetite, bad taste in the mouth, and completely prostrated at frequent inter- vals with the most agonizing attacks from congestion and the passage of gravel, ootaining but transient relief from talented medical meo. I was completely broken down physically, and firmly of the opinion, which was shared by my friends, that I should never regain my heal th,as during my long residence in India the kidneys and liver had be- come so diseased that I was beyond permanent relief. "While in this desponding condition, I was one day talk- ing with my friend Mr. D. L. M. Moore, of 3, Hill-street, S.W.. when he called my attention to a paragraph in the Christian Union. a paper at that time edited by the late Henry Ward Beecher, which recounted a certain investiga- tion which had been made regarding a remedy for the cure of kidney and liver oiseases, at that time attracting a great deal of attention in the United States. I decided to try the medicine, and procured it at once. The first dose gave me relief, and under its cantinued user rapidly improved. In ' ten months I fully recovered my health, and am to-day in its full and perfect enjoyment, never having had a particle of trouble since my remarkable recovery. As this was five years ago, I can safely say that It is all to be attribu- ted to Warner's Sane Cure,' a medicine which I consider has no peer for all diseases of the kidneys and liver. It has given me a new lease of life. It is a remedy, I think, par- ticularly designed for climates such as diat of India, and I hops soon to near that steps have been taken which will enable the inhabitants of that country to receive benefits from its use.
" Yours faithfully, W. F. NCTRALL, General. h 10,_1Edirla Terme-, &Hill Grove, _ _

I le, and their technical Imowledg'e gave them in very many instances a commanding position, and enabled them to cheapen their cost of manufac- ture very considerably. (Hear, hear.) -He believed that technical education would also tend to make the artisans of this country more thoughtful, more industrious, and altogether lift them in the scale of education. He had expressed • a certain amount of disappointment at the former effort made on behalf of a school of 'science. That effort was not so suc- cessful as they could have wished, but if there was a feeling in the town to renew that effort, be for one would not be behind his fellow townsmen in promoting its success. (Hear, hear.) He musts however, say that his recent experience had led him to look to the taking up of that question in an ele- mentary form rather than in the form in which they formerly took it up. lie hoped that the teach- ing of technical knowledge in its rudimentary or elementary stages would be taken up in the elemen- tary schools of the town, so that children might be familiarised with the sui3ject as they grew up, and those who had the taste for these subjects shall be graded into other schools, and so find their way to some school in connection with the museum or school of art, and the best of them put in the posi- tion to go on with the education. It might be pos- sible to make such arrangements with the Victoria University that the learners could be sent to Man- chestei or Liverpool. It had been named to him that it might be suggested to Sir Andrew Walker, who had given a very munificent donation to Liver- pool college for the establishment of a chemical laboratory, that lie should attach a condition to this gift that the professors of that college should be called upon to give lectures in Warrington free of any charge. (Hear, hear.) lie (Mr. Monks) thought that was a very good suggeston, made to him by his friend Mr. W. Owen, and he thought lie might mention it there that night. (Applause.) Mr. DIGGLB. in seconding Mr. Monks' proposition, said he had had experience in connection with. one of the largest works in Warrington, and he found that whenever they wanted anybody with technical knowledge they had to go out of the town for him. Mr. Diggle also suggested that landowners who drew large sums of money from Warrington and others who had made their fortunes in the town and then left it should be asked to subscribe. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) THE WALL IN SANSEY-STREET. Alderman HARBISON moved that any balance that might remain after defraying the cost of the proces- sion should be applied to the-removing of the wall in front of the Town Hall, and to the laying out of Bower beds and the erecting of seats and a fountain. He thought this would be a very desirable improve- ment to be carried out, and he mentioned that Sir Gilbert Greenall had offered to give a very hand- some fountain on condition that the wall was pulled down. (Hear, hear.) , Mr. JOLLEY seconded the proposiiion. Mr. Jodie RkincLoyear said he had no doubt the , taking down of the wall would belt greet improve-. ment, but he, thought it was more of a ratepayers' matter, and if it were done it should be done by thel town. (Hear;lear.) The Mayon; in supporting, the motion, said that ()lie of the objects they should pave ,most in view in connection with the Jubilee fund waa something that was for the enjoyment of every one in the , town, man, woman, and child. (Hear; hear.) He • did not think they should have it large enough . balance in hand after the expenses of the-procession , were paid for to build a technical school' or enlarge . the baths or do. anything of that kind; but they , might possibly have a small balances which, he thought could not' be put to a better Vurpose than • taking dbwn the wall. The matter had been, before the Corporation for some years, but it had always been thought that it would be too great a eti arge on the ratepayers. He also mentioned that Sir Gilbert Greenall had promised to give a handsome fountain if the plan of pulling the wall down were-adopted. (Applause.) THE BATHS. Mr, H. ROBERTS -moved that any surphis- remain- ing after the procession should be applied to the ex- tension Of, the boths. A good deal had been said about the advisability and the desimbilityof taking down the wall in front of the Town Hall, and as .to the fact that that would greatly improve the pro- perty at that portion of the street he had not -one ' word to say in contradiction. Indeed, he-believed all that had been said in that reapect to be perfectly true, but he claimed for his proposition that it -had reference to what was not merely ornamental, but useful. He claimed that they could better celebrate Her Majesty's Jubilee by applying thateurplus fund to that which is useful than to that which is orna- mental only. He claimed priority for his ,Proposal on that account. While he had not been able- to obtain a majority on the sub-committee,. the °unani- mous opinion of the seb-committee had been thou it , was a desirable thing that his proposal should be: carried out by the ratepayers if not by that Jubilee, fund. (Hear, bean) .And if they decided against his proposal that night lie should be prepared: to bring it before the Council to obtain their selection, which' he hoped would be backed out by the rate- payers generally.-. It had be, mentioned thet , there were something like eight: thousand children attending school in Warrington, and in•act- dition there were three or four thousand' who had left school, so that they had a constituency of 12,000 or 13,000 young people, not one of whom-had the opportunity of learning within the limits of the borough that great desideratum—to swim. (110ar, , hear.) Our present baths are utterly inadequate to- provide for anything like the number of People that ought to be enabled to use them. Not only that, but tbey were in such a condition as to be very un- pleasant the greater portion of the • time they are , open, and their sanitary surroundings are objection- able. There was also nothing in the shape of Turkish baths which he did. think it was desirable to have, and a small expense would' make the baths complete in this respect. (Applause.) Mr. Joinmseconded Mr. Roneter'e proposal.. THE FREE LIBRARY.' ' Mr. T. Monms•moved that any balance reniaining- . from the procession should be applied to making the- • library a free lending library. He contended thafr . lads who were just leaving school, those between. • the ages of 14 and 21, should be: able to go to-the library and get a book out of it to read and consult.. • It might be said'that a penny a/ week was•a small ; sum to pay as subscription, and if they-could pay' • the subscriptien by a penny a, week it might do • very well; but al man could not go to the library • with a penny; he mush have the Is &Tor nothing, . and Is 6d they knew would often keep, the bread and cheese out of the oupboard. (Hear, hear.) The •' fact that so many school children had to have their fees paid for them ont'of the rates was. a proof that ,- the parents could not afford La pay for the books out of the library. (Hear, hear.) Mn Morris also • referred to the fact that people who were not rate- payers by paying the subscription got books from the library which was mainly kept up .by the rates . which the working-men of the, totem were paying. • He-said it MR not righteous; it was not fain (A p- • plause.) . • Mr. J. WA:tarEn seconded' Mr. Morris's proposal. 1143 said that some of those who advocated the free- ing of the library felt that, it was an injustice that after paying their rates they should be called upon a second time. They felt that having paid for the .thing in, the shape of a rate which was the legi- timate and legal way, they ought not to be asked to pay for the use of the books, but to have them free • as they had in other towns. They thought also thatthis was a fitting thing for steps to be taken to gAt this thing carried out. He could claim fbr the object he advocated that it might be said to have her Majesty's sanction, Looking through a memoir of the Queen's life he happened to stumble upon a letter written by direction of her reas=, which he would take the opportunity of

"Buckingham Palace, Oet., 1873. Sir,-1 am desired to acknowledge your letter to the Queen, with a statement relative to Mr. John Elllett's in- vention for issuing books, and a statement of the Wolverhamptoa Free Library. I Mn to say that her Majesty is always gratified, at bearing of any plans by which additional facilities and inducements aro afforded to the working classes to make use of public libraries, and her Majesty is pleased to know that in so thickly popu- lated a district as that lriag around Wolverhampton such facilities exist, and are apparently so much awe- dated by the class for whom the libraries have been establisbed.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient , servant, T. M. BIDDIMPH. Mr. W. H. DARKIN." (Hear, hear.) They iii Warrington had the books—they had some 20,000 volumes,—they had the staff, and they had the institution with a penny rate raising some .E5OO or £6OO a year. The carrying out of their object was simply a matter of arrangement, and might be done by a few people laying their heads together. It had been said that that was not a jubilee object, but people elsewhere were making it a jubilee object. That very night the people of Leigh were meeting Mr the purpose of promoting such an object, and at Altrincham the 'same step was being taken. They had a Free Lend- , ing Library at Widnes, Runcorn, Wigan. and other 1 neighbouring towns, and he thought it was scarcely creditable to Warrington that it had nct been done

there. They ought to do the best they could to wipe away the reproach, and to do it in such away that it would be a graceful thing in the Jubilee year. (Applause.) Mr. 11. WHIT/EAU claimed that he knew some- thing of the feeling of working-men generally, and he could assure those present that the one thing they would regard as a boon would be that they could go to the institution in Bold-street and take out a book free of cost. The statement that a penny a week was a small sum had been noticed by Mr. Morris, but the fact was they could not get a book for a penny if they took it. He himself had asked at the library if there was no means by which a man might bring a guarantee, and be allowed to take an expensive book on the payment of a small sum, and he was told thete was not. While that question had been in agitation he had noticed re- ferences to [novel reading. Well, the people were more or less what the teacher made them, and the committee who had the selection of books were notcompelled to spend all their money on novels, nor were they forced to buy "trashy novels.!' He held that the reading of a good novel would injure n,o one. He also said, and he said it with all res- pect, that-the charge about the working-man read- ing novels came with tr very bad grace from those who made it, for if they looked in their own homes and saw what class of books their own wives and daughters took from the library they would find that a very large percentage was novels. (Hear, hear, and lhughter.) The habit of reading amongst the working classes wanted encouraging, and if they were given every opportunity of reading a. good book the town would very likely be im— mensely benefited, and the labours of our magis-- trates reduced. (Hear, hear.) A free library was an institution that would help them in competition with the world. On the continent a free library always worked.alongside the technical school. If they put a workman in a technical school it was necessary that he should know what he was stri- ving against in the shape of foreign competition, and how could he know, unless he reads the works that gave him that information, and he could only see these works if they came to him free. He held that the greatest need of the dity was the establish- ment of Free Libraries, and these lead to the Tech- nical School. Ho should like to see both be- come permanent institutions int Warrington. (Ap- plause.)

Alderman HARRISON thought that Mr. Whitham should have told them that anyone could go to the library now, and have the most expeneive book it contained, if he would be content to read it in the library, and that such a thing as an absolutely free lending library did not exist in this country. There was always a reference department in con- nection with libraries, containing valuable books that it would be most unwise to allow to be taken off the premises. If the views suggested were carried out there would still be a reference library. (A voice : We understand that.) He was sure that no one was more anxious than he was that that they should have a free lending library—(" oh "I —and he hoped that the gentlemen to be appointed to meet the Library Committee would receive the most respectful con- sideration on the part of that committee. He believed that there was not a member of the committee who would wil- lingly curtail the utility of a free lending library, providing that it was compatible with the interests of the Museum and Art Gallery. Mr. Morris and M. Walker spoke of what other towns did in the establishment of free lending libraries, but the bulk of them had not to support a valuable museum such as they in Warrington possessed. When Warrington toek advantage of the Free Libraries' Act, in- stnd of confining themselves simply to a lending library they adopted the Museum and Art Gallery. There WAS ' such a liability yet attaching to those institutions that it seemed difficult to find any scheme by which they could do what had been suggested and keep out of debt. The Library Committee was considerably in debt in consequence of the money spent upon the buildings. If some of them did not vote for the scheme it was not becinse they did not approve of it, hut because they wished to vote for the schemes that were the most feasible.

Mr WHITIIAM : We hold that no stuient• can study a book when ho is at the library. The reading room does not help a student in his work. What he wants,io be have the books by his own fireside. The Maxon : Studen's study at the museum in London. Mr. Witruratr : But they are— scholara) and are used to it.

Mr. F. MONKS Paid he did not agree with Mr. Harrison that there was no such thing as a Free Library. There were—should he say scores ?--of free libraries in the sense in which he understood that Mr. Morris and his friends wished the library in Warrington to be free. (Hear, hear.) Hp had never heard anyclaimmade for lending out the books in the reference library, and he had heard further that when a proposition was made that the circulating subscription library should be limited, say, to twAve, months, that was an idea they fell in with readily. As far as he understood, Mr. Morris did not prepose- that any naocey should be t Ikea from the Jubilee fund, but his proposition was con- fined to a recommendation from that committee, which, he imagined, Mr. Morris thought would have considerable weight. The suggestion that a deputation should wait upon the Library Committee to consider the question, and nee if they o,mlcl not Clad a solution of it, seemed to him to be one in which they would all agree. Mr. Ilawerwrr said that the resolution was quite contrary to what Mr. Monks supposed. Mr. MORRIS said that he believed that, with the influence of the conAittee, they would obtain what they wanted without touching a penny of the demonstration fund. Mr. WALKER suggested that a vete be taken on the free lending library question as well as on the others. If that failed it would be open to the committee to pursue the Other course.

Mr. A. R&THBONE said that be•should like to vote for a technical school, and should also like a com- mittee to be appointed to wait upon the Library Committee. It appeared to him that Alderman Har- rison had taken a course that would make it evident thit he was protesting his friendship to this scheme too much. lie had taken every opportunity that had presented itself of throwing cold water upon it, and his course of ncw professing friendship was a strange one. (Hear, bear.) He (Mr. Rathbone) thought that if the library were made free it would prove of material assistance towards the ultimate formation of a technical School.

div.head: JUBILEE TEMPERANCE MISSIONS.
div.p: JUBILEE TEMPERANCE MISSIONS.

On Wednesday evening, what was called an 1.0.G.T. Jubilee Mission, was commenced in the Temperance Mission Room, Academy-street, War- rington. Brother Hall presided, and there was a fairly good attendance. In opening the meeting, the Chairman said that one of the objects they had in view was to place before the public the importance of the aims of the Good ,Templars. The lodge to which he be- longed had, he mentioned, met for between fifteen or sixteen years in thaf room every Wednesday evening, and he had been connected with it for thirteen years out of that period. They were still continuing the work, and must continue it vigorously. At the close of the meeting there would be, a lodge session, at which they would be glad to initiate teetotalers as members: those who were not teetotillers were asked to sign the pledge, and afterwards to join the lodge.—Brother WRITHALL, of Barrow, Home Missionary to the Good Templar Order, then delivered a stirring tem- perance address. He premised his remarks by the statement that what is socially and morally wrong, cannot be leeally right, and then went on to show that the existence of the drink traffic as it is in this country at pre- sent Is to all intents and purposes the greatest curse of the nation. They affirmed, he said, without fear of contradiction, that Its disturbing influences reached the community and the nation, that it disturbed first the social relationships of the family, and then of the community by increasing, directly or indirectly. its tssation. It diminished the wealth and crippled the industry of a nation. It was said that the traffic employed 800,000 persons, but he con- tended that if the money absorbed by the traffic were inves- ted in legitimate commerce it WOula give employment to two million people. The trade was a huge menopoly, worked at an immense profit, and, in this time of long con- tinued depression working-men should ponder over this qiiestion, and ask themselves how much of the money spsnt on drink finds its way back into the labour market. No government, he urged, had the right to continue the exis- tence of this traffic. The question of revenue should not stand in the way of such a reform; there was no such thing as "vested interest" in a nation's curses. A. license was a twelvemonths privilege, and nothing more. The people were ready for legislation on this abject, and legis- lation they must have. Mr. Wrathall, whose address was listened to with interest, was he trtily applauded. During the evening hymns ware given by the choir.

JUBILEE.
COMMITTEE MEETING.

: - A meeting of the committee appointed to take into consideration the various schemes -proposed for celebrating the Queen's Jubilee was held. on Mon- day evening in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall. Mr. F. Monks presided, and the Other gentle- men present were the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alderman Harrison, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Dr. Fox, Rev. J. A. .Drummond. Rev. ft. F. Roberts, Major Bolton, and Messrs. T. Morris, T. Birchall, J. Walker, H. Roberts, T: W. Bennett, J. Smethurst, T. Birtles, T. Roberts, C. Tvriss, W. Unsvrorth, J. E. Wright, R. W. Franconab, A. 'Rathbone, J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk.)—The CHAIR- MAN said that owing to a mishap he believed Mr. Morris did not get his notice of the previous meeting of the committee until the following-morn- ing, and therefore in fairness to Mr. Morris and Mr. Walker they would leave the discussion °pee to hear what they had to say that night.—Mr. T. NORRIS then dealt with the, library scheme, and suggested that that committee might form a sub-committee to be called a special or-Jubilee sub-committee, to. con- sider the ways and means of making the library a free lending one. He would suggest that that sub- committee consisted of six members of the Library and Museum Committee, and the following six The Rev. S. Wilkinson, the Rev. J. Yonge, Mesas. F. Monks, J. Roberts; J. Walker, and either Mr. J. Gaudy or himself. The reason for making this re- quest was that if this committee were ' formed he believed that he would be able to lay such material lbefore the twelve gentlemen that on the 21st June next our public library would be a free lend- ing one. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Morris then re- ferred to the case of Preston, where they IMBRD- tained a free lending library, a museum and an art gallery, with a penny rate and in a single year they had saved .£3OO. out of the proceeds of the rate. If there were difficulties in Warrington in making the penny rate cover all the expenses- he could give the names of a number of gentlemenwho would continue their subscriptions, and by this means £.20 or £3O could' be annually raised. (Hear, hear.)—Mr;Jorm WALKER supported Mr. Mor's suggestion, and remarked that the appointment of a committee would be an easy way of carrying that matter a bit further. In his own mind there were three or four ways in which . the freeing, of the library might be done, but as yet it had never been brought to;anything like a determinate issue, and if they got a committee appointed they might go into the thing in detail. par, hear.)—lt -was then deeided to adopt Mr.. Morris's suggestion, and to in- clude it in the report of the Committee. —ln the course of some further conversation cheeMioron said that he understood from whet the Mnyoress said that she and the.ladies were going to•provide medals for the school children; at all events the Mayoress would see that the children have them. (hear, hear.)—The following report vraa adopted by the committee for presentation to the general meet- ing, viz.:—" The sub-committed appointed' to con- sider the best way of celebrating the Jubilee of her Majesty's accesion to the throne, have fully con- sidered the several objects which have been pro- posed. The subjects which were discussed were :- 1, making of the library into a free lending library.; 2, extending the public baths; 3, pulling clown the wall in front of the Town Hall and laying out the land ; 4, establishing a ragged school ; 5, hold- ing an exhibition of local manufactures; 6, es- tablishing technical schools; 7, erecting cabmen's shelters. On the several propositions being put to the vote there appeared in favour of technical schools, 19; removing wall, 18; extension of baths, 16 ; free library; 14 ; ragged schools, 6: The other propositions were withdrawn. The Committee con- sider that the primar3. object of the, celebration should be the procession of trades, societies, and children, already decided upon by the general com- mittee. The procession should be fully representa- tives of professions, trades, friendly and other so- cieties, and schools and inhabitants.. The-arrange- ments must be left to special sub-committees. A suggestion has been made that a medal be struck, and distributed among the children instead of any money payment to the schools, and this the sub- committee might consider. We estimate the fol-' lowing sums would be required to, carry out the schemes proposed :—The procession, which shust be a first charge on the fund, ZOO.; ,technical schools, .£6OO to £7OO to starji with, having free use of the lecture room at the museum and the labora- tory returned, but £2,000 at least if a new buil& i ing sto be erected; removing wall £500; baths, estimated cost, £2,000 to -£3,000.4 ' The' Committee recommended the appointment of a sub-committee of six to consider the question of snaking the library a free lending •library.—Mr. BIRCIULL moved, and the Rev. J. A. Dnemmosen seconded, the adoption of the report, which was agreed tb.—This concluded the business of the Committee, GENERAL MEETING. . _ _

Afterwards a general meeting of those who had been invited by the Mayor to consider. the matter of the jubilee was held in the Council Chamber. The Mayor presided, and in addition to the gentle- men present at the committee meeting 'reported above, there was a considerable _attendance.
_ The' report agreed upon by the Committee was read, and its adoption was moved by Mr. F. MONKS, seconded by Mr. J. WALKER.

incurncAL sortoor. Mr. F. Moxim then moved that any balance left over after defraying the expenses of and incidental to the procession be applied to the formation of a Technical School. In advocating that scheeme he said he was looking to the interests of Warrington in the future, and because he believed that the question of technical education is one that should be seriously taken up with a view to promoting our industries, and holding our own. in competition with the world. (Hear, hear.) Those who were engaged in business knew how closely the foreigners,-and particularly those of the continent, are upon the heels of English manufacturers. There was an estimate given of £5OO. .11e. wanted. to know whether, if they did not get the £5OO the schema would fall through, and what would be done with the money that had been raised?. He did not want them to do the work badly for want of bode. He would give something to the Jubilee Fund—but with a better heart to some of the other schemes—although he was willing to go with the majority; but not unless the scheme could be properly carrie3 out: He did not believe in spend- ing £lOO mendv to take down the wall. The Mayon (in reply) said that all the schemes were almost in the clouds as to expense, hut he got the Borough Surveyor to look into the matter as far as the removal of the wall is concerned, aad he suggested that £4(10 would be sufficient. THE LIBRA= SCHEME. It was then unanimously resolved, on the motion of the MAYOR, csoconded by Mr. Famicoara, that the am 8. Wil- kinaon, the Rev. John Yonge, and Messrs. T. Morris, J 4 Walker, P. Monty,. and J. Roberts be appointel ajCommit- tee to act in conjunction with the Library and Museum Cornmittne with a view to devising some plan for freeing the Library during the Jubilee year.

GENERAL ARRANGEMENTS. The MAYOR at this point intimated that the Mayoress intended to call a meeting to see if they could carry out the propoml to provide the school children with medals. He did not think there would be any difficulty in reference to that matter. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Parma said that many people connected with friendly societies in the town had been disappointed at not having received invitations to the meetings of the Jubilee Committee. Nearly all the friendly societies would shortly --in about a fortnight—be holding their district meetings, at which they were going to decide what they would do. As chairman of one of the societies he should be pleased to call a meeting to carry out a suggestion that had been made —pat the friendly societies thould send delegates to a working committee to be appointed. Mr. DEWHERST raised the question as to Walking Day, and as to whether money would, be supplied from the gene rat fund for school treats on the Jubilee day. It was ex- plained that details of that kind were for further considera- tion, but that it was the general opinion that it would be beat to put off Walking Day this year till the Jubilee cele- bration.

It was then resolved, on the motion of Mr. MONKS, se- conded by Mr. J. E. Witrenvr, that delegates from the various friendly societies, trade societies, Sunday schools, and other societies intending te take part in the Jubilee de- monstration, with the sub-committee already appointed, form the general committee, with power to add to their number. It was also resolved that Mr. Blackhurst and Mr S. E. Johnson be nomicated members of the Committee to represent the shop-keeping interest of the town. It was further decided that the first meeting of the general committee be held on Monday week, at seven o'clock in the evening, and that due notice thereof be given bv advertisement. .

Warrisgton, March 24, 1887. _ A GYMNASIUM FOR WARRINGTON.

Sir,--Please allow roe most cordially to endorsa the opinions exp,el9ed in a letter nneer the above heeding, that appeared in your issue of last Saturday. That a gym- nasium is much needed in a town like Warrington goes without saying, and "T. W.'s" suggestion that a powerful organisation like the Football Club is a body most likely to manage one with success is an excellent one. A gymnasium would prove a good training ground for the footballert, by which they could do much to keep up their splendid phy- sique, and at the same time it would prove. if thrown open to them, a boon to a large number ef the pnblic, whose subscriptions wonld go along way towards paying expenses.

RUNCORN AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. Sir,—Seeing my name brought forward in a letier upon the jubilee meeting in Runcorn, signed " Nonconformist," I write to say how much I regret any false impreesion con- nected with the subject. But "Nonconformist " has cer- tainly been misinformed, for the circulars I sent eut were sent from a list of names given to me, and included the names of several of the Nonconformist ladies in Runcorn ; but only one of them attended the meeting. I much regret if any who were willing to work were omitted. Requesting you will kindly allow this letter to appear in your neat edition, I remain yours truly, HENRItTT% G. BROOKE. Norton Priory, Runcorn, March 23d, 1887. ILady Brooke's explanation is a very satisfactory one, and it is to be hoped it will be the means of removing any misapprehension that may have arisen.—En. ix.]

A PAUPERBI WAITING-LOOM. Sir,—Passing daily along one of our widest thorough- fares, not ten miles distant from the old &lurch," I have Many times during this inclement weather noticed outside the premises of a parish doctor groans of shivering wretched- . . _ . . . .

looking patients waiting burr bly- for admission: the cheer- . littleness of their lot being in no way drcreased by a glimpse through the CTOPO adjoining window into the cony drawing. room (all aglow with ruddy light) of the parish official re- ferred to. At the prowl. (P) time admission-is given to a aide entry, one end of which is made up partly by a door overtopped by iron grating. the other ena being entirely ex- posed to the element, and it is into this miserable fraud of a waiting-room (through which the bi,ing drnughts rush keen and cold) that delicate iitt pauper invalids are ushered from the street, and where oa a form they are ranged until singly called into the siirprry for medicine or for treatment. Surely our guardians of the poor are not cognisant of this celd uncharitable method of dispenaing medical charity.— Yours, &c., HUMANITY. Warrington, March 22nd, 1897.

THE EX•MAYOR re ALDERMAN HARRISON. you allow me a few words open this subject, although the unimportance of the question raised hardly merits notice? What can it matter to any tidman being where the ex-Mayor at the "double ex-Mayor " sits in the Council, but there being a chair appointed for the ex-lVlavor to sit in, who cm have a greater right to stt in it than Alderman Harrison? He is de facto, and de jure the ex- Mayor. He was " Maror " last year and must be " ex- Mayor " this year Poor Doctor Mackie was appointed mayor, it is true, in November last, and be was an appointed for a year as the law directs, but in less than a month afterwards he became disqualified by his unfortunate affiic- tion, and resigned without-ever having been able to dis- charge the duties. How then can be be regarded as the ex- Mayor, except in the most technitia/ sense? The ex-Mayer, remains a borough magistrate fora year after ebb expira- tion of his mayoral rear; hat if Dr. Mackie get better, and was able to resume his seat in the Council, he would not be a borough magistrate for a day, because be ' failed to dis- charge the duties of ‘lavor, for which 1 e was appointed. I am quite of Alderman Eiarrison's opinion that your Corres- pondent" Boxer," in raising such a question, could only have been prompted to do so by peevishness, which is not creditable to any man who indulges such propensities. The ex-Mayor is only a title of courtesy, and not recognised by law, and surely if after a man has served the town as its Mayor for three censecutive years so satisfactorily as Alder- man Harrison has done, he Es entitled to any mark of caurtesv which custom may have established.—l am, sir, yours, LC.,
J. T. W.

THE Juin.EN CELEBRATION 1I WARRINGTON. 1314—At the meeting oft the, sub-committee on Monday last, Mr. Harrison, in speaking in favour of the removal of the wall in front of the Town Hall is reported to have raid: *They had a Town Hall they need be proud of, but at the present time it was biAden from view, and strangers coming Into Warrington did not know that they had a To Hall at aIL" Hark! ts the hurrled question of despair. Where's are TOW)11 Hall? an echo answen "Where?" I am !lorry my idPas of the beautiful do not Coincide with those evidently entertained by Mr. Harrison in respect to the Bank Park structure. To my mind distance lends enchant. men, to the view, and I am afraid the mere removal of the obnoxious 'LW will not be the means of enlightening strangers that Warringtln really possesses a Tows Hall. As a public le iilding the strectore has no claim to beauty, and r am sadly afraid its plainness will become more apparent when placed in controd with the architectural grandeur of the fountain 80 kindly promised by Sir Gilbert Greenall. A friend of mine whom I was aceempanying to Bank Quay station a few weeks ago, noiming to the Town Hall inquired if it was the Workhouse or a Lunatic Asylum, and on my I explaining the real character of the building he fairly

It was clearly pointed out at the meeting held in the Town Hall, last Monday evening, that the penny in the pound rate that is now paid would still be sufficient to meet the requirements of carrying on the library, if made free. Ratepayers would then be at liberty to obtain books there- from to take home and read at their leisere, precisely as at Wigan, Preston, and other towns where Free Libraries are established. Now, Sir, we are told that we do not want the use of the books, and that we do not appreciate the suggested scheme. I scarcely need remind you of tile enthusiasm of the Meet- ing that took place in the Co-operative Hall a few weeks I ago, called bv the deputy-mayor, when almost ever hand was held up in favour of the library being made free at a purely working-men's meeting. I feel certain if the same test was taken throughout the whole of the town we should find the same response that we received at that meeting. The working-class..e are determined not to allow this opportunity I to slip by, but will rally round those who have so gener- ously come forward in their interest and show them they appreciate their labours. Hoping the committee that was suggested on Monday night will be the means of bringing the matter to a success- ful issue,—l am, yours truly. .
A WORKING-MAN.

"REMEMBER DIGOLE." Sir,—A letter in your last issue, signed "Remember Die- gle," was "very entertaining reading," and at least one part of it "must hove provoked tee mirth of all thoughtful people." I do not object to your cor- respondent's advocacy of a Technical School, which, were it foend practicable, I should of all things like to see carried out, but I do most certainly ob- ject to his nonsensical sentence—" How sad it is to see our young men going mad over foothill, and spending their evenings at street corners blinding themselves with tobacco smoke, just because no nobler ways of spending their time are provided." Probably I should misconstrue "Remember Diggle" if I thought be meant to insinuate that it is the footballers who spend their evenings in the manner he mentions, but it is hard to see where the saeness comes in when we find young men taking a pleasure in healthy and manly bxlily exercise, that is in itself calculated to better it them for mental pursuits. A man who can hold his own in a football field has learnt the value et energy, applica- tion, and determination. and is fully as likely to hold his own at a technical school as the milksops who have not the pluck to go in for any manly recreation. "Remember Dig- gle " surely forgets that there is a time for play as well as work. As regards the misguided who blind themselves with tobacco smoke at street corners, does he actually think that cornermen would be the persons to take advantage of a Technical School? I think not. There are nobler ways, if they chose to find them, of spending their time, even in Warrington. The elms be refers to, as a class, would not be bribed to join a Technical School, or, if they did join, would be no credit to either the school or themselves, and they would still prefer the pipe and the street corner. With the exception of his nasty hit at football, and his seeming idea that cornermen who blind themselves with tobacco smoke would patronise a technical school, lon the whole agree with the tone of your correspondent's remarks, but as a smoker myself, I would give him the information that those foolish mortals who take a pleasure in the fragrant weed, are not in the habit of " blieding themselves " either at street corners or anywhere else.—Youre. kc., March 23rd 1887. div.head: FOOTBALL-WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.
div.p: FOOTBALL-WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.

_ Sir,—Some very ugly rumours are in circulation bearing on our defeat by Wigan last Saturday. With a view to restoring the confidence in their hitherto favourites; I should like to call the attention of the public to a few facts which to my mind are quite sufficient to account for the game end- ing as it did. Io the first place, we were unfortunate in being without the services of Gilbert and W. Dillon. two of the very b‘st players in the club, and a man bad to be drafted out of the A team to take Gilbert's place who was almost totally un- used to the play of the first team. Then Jolley'e ankle, which we thought had got quite strong, again gave way during the game, and for some tims we were playing a man short, and two of our forwards, as it turned out afterwards, pluckily, but foolishly, rather than lose their places in the team, played with ailments which prevented them showing anything like their usual form. When we take into con- sideration that the great bulk of the spectators seized every opportunity of showing that they were bitterly hostile to Warrington, and that the Wigan backs were exceptionally heavy and powerful, there is perhaps an excuse for some of our light backs not playing with their usual dash ad pluck. My object in penning these lines is not to excuse our , defeat, but to show there are ample legitimate reasons to attribute our defeat to, without giving credence to the un- founded rumours afioat. Our team is naturally depressed through their defeat by a team which they have so easily beaten on previous occa- sions, but they will, I feel confident, turn up to a man for the next match, which takes place on April 2nd, bent on retrieving their somewhat tarnished reputation. I trust our supporters will be there in force, and bearing in mind the brilliant exploits our team has performed during this and last season, will give them such a reception 39 will put new life into them and spur them on to make strenuous efforts to regain that proud position in the football world from which they bave,.l ant confident, been only temporarily deposed.-4 remain, yours truly, I. E. WARREN, Hon. Sec. Warrington P.C.

div.head: THOUGHT 3 ON MR. PEERS' "THOUGHTS."
div.p: THOUGHT 3 ON MR. PEERS' "THOUGHTS."

Bir,—l thank you for allowing me to reply once more to Mr. Peers. lam glad that Mr. Peers accepts my letter as the honest expression of my opinions, and I freely ext-nd the same courtesy to him. lam sorry he should think I got into a rage. In this be was quite mistaken, as. I assure hirm my normal temperature was not in the least increased by the perusal of hi&" thoughts." He need not be at all nervous about me. . . . .

_ I notice that he abandons his positions on Anthropology and Evolution, aad pins me down hard and fast to Chrono- logy. He accuses me of "trying to tinker the word of God so as to make it square with the revelations of science." Now, sir, I did no ouch thing; neither have I attempted to "pare and shape" the statements of Moses. If he will take the trouble to read my letter again he will find that I merle no mention of the six days—nor yet of any " is- definite periods," Neither did I attempt to mutilate and stultify the Word of God. Ought I net rather to say "Thou art the man?" and, tasteful of bins asking the silly question, " has it required the lapse of all these desolate centuries and.,the appearance d such luminaries as Daw- son, Gaudy, &Co ," ought he let to have said—it has re., qdired the lapse or all these desolate centuries and the ap- pearance of such luminaries as Darwin, Spencer, Peers, dr . .

to expound this text to the world? But it is ever the habit of certain dabblers in science to decry the intelligence of those who differ from them. I like that remark of his about "these poor people." It is so modest and considerate of him, you know. Now as to these actual facts of geology and the statement of Moses. Cannot Mr. Peers see that these said facts—so called—are merely assumptions? Can he sanely contend that one mind in ten thousand, or one in a hundred thousand, can ascertain these facts for himself? Are they capable of demonstration with the exactness of Euclid? And can they ever to the vast majority of minds be anything more than mere statements? And since cosmogony and its sister sciences are the subjects of the first chapter of the Bible. would Mr. Peers—as a kind of preparatory course—make Darwinian and Spencerian philosophers of men before teach- ing them the truth of religion ? Now the moral of all this is.—don't dogmatize. Scientists,. no more than theologians, have any excuse for doing so. Science is still in its infancy, and has many surprises yet in store for us. The one hope for science is mere science. Bacon says—" This I dare affirm in knowledge of natn-e, that a little na'ural philosophy, and the first entrance into It. does dispose the opinion to Atheism ; but, on the other side, much uctural philosophy, and deep wading into it, will bring about men's minds to religion." I Now I quite agree with Mr. Peers that it is not essential to true religion that a man should believe in the Mosaic account of the creation. The beauty and morality of re- ligion can not, in my opinion, be lessened by any discoveries of science. But all the same, I maintain that Mosee has not yet been disproved. Eminent authorities are not want- ing who affirm that tbs account of the creation as given by ' Mines Is exactly in accordance with modern theories. The six days may be only an allegory, bnt to me it is quite im- material whether a man believes in six days or six periods. As to the Sabbath, I certainly believe its origin was divine. In any cane. I gratefully accept it as a fact. It has been a priceless boon to myriads upon myriads of the human family, and is certainly not indebted for its origin to 'lux. Icy, Tyndal, and Co. Now. lam not unmindful of, nor do I under estimate, the splendid services these men have ren- dered to the cause of science, but I cannot join issue with , them in their materialistic and evolutionist views. I In conclusion, it is not true that Hugh Miller "Fought refuge in suicide from the difficulties of reconciling the un- doubted facts of geology with the statements of Moses." Irritation of the brain, brought on by protracted inflamma- tion of the lungs, was the cause of his suicide. He is still Considered an authority by geologists well abreast of the times. Warrington.
