Er.] REASONS WHY WE SHOULD BE JUBILANT. Sir,—l suppose we should all be able to give a reason for the conclusions that guide us all in our .dallv life, Allow
%yor

Fonblanque, in his work, gives us a number of maxims respecting the sovereign, amongst which we are told that she is supreme head of the State, the Church, the army, the navy," its. It is well for the nation these are only maxims; any attempt to carry them beyond that point would most likely eand disastrously for the sovereign. Tkere is no need to trace the evolution of the monarchical system from its earliest days of barbarism. We know it is the offspring of brute force and ambition; that it has in all ages, and all nations, waded through blood. We see its history in the ruins of empires and fallen kingdonss. In the Church and King riots of last century and the Church and King worshippers of to-day, we have one constant struggle to beat off oppression. Its emblems are the rampant Lion and the ferocious Eagle, and we in England find ourselves to-day face to face with two significant featnres, viz., a sovereign who insists on foisting her German relatives upon the English taxpavcr, and the German workman who is ground down by an Imperial Bismarkian system, second to none in its despotic attempt to make brute force rule over mind.

It,is said to be mean when men grumble at the cost of royalty, end America is pointed at as being no more economi- cal than ourselves. I have not sufficient room to make the comparison, so must keep to cur own beautiful system. During the fifty years her Majesty has condescended to reign over us, she has kindly received, per Civil List, Duchy of Lancaster, Ancient Fee, and Compensatory Annuity, near upon £23,000,000. This is very kind on her part, and should make us thankful. Her " dear " son, the Prince of Wales, since he came of age, has received, drat, his yearly salary, £160,000, next, from the Duchy of Cornwall, £1,508,000, and a Compensatory Annuity. £290,538, or a total of near £3,000,000. What a deal we have to be thankful for, to be sure. Next we have the royal household, palaces, parks, yachts, troops. I will leave out the amount, Mr. Editor; the brain becomes confused amongst so many figures. I will merely say that millions of good money have during these glorious fifty years been spent on the above and upon "up- holsterers and cabinet makers." But her Majesty is chari- table—yes, we give her, in England, for charitable purposes, £13,000; Scotland, £1500; Ireland, £300; for her Majesty's racing plate (England), £1500; Scotland, £2lB. Who couldn't be charitable on such easy terms, especially in Ire- land? It certainly is amusing to hear some of our royalty admirers talk. They seem to assume that when we have paid the trifle of £385000 we have done. In 1880 the country paid £ll,OOO for conveyance by sea of the royal household, and we are quite accustomed to paying, fcr single trips across the channel, for various members of the dear family, the sum of £4O. Nrhen the Prince of Wales' eldest son was kn:ghted, he being rather hard up, we chari- tably paid £548 for the little job. We sent the royal gentleman on a trip to fndia with a cheque for £142,000, and quietly buried his brother, the Doke of Albany, for the small sum of 42,725. Her Majesty keeps, or the nation does, three cooks, who unequally divide amongst them £2,100 a year. So that these may not be too hard worked, we give them eighteen assistaats, at a cost not stated. We vote annually large sums for bread, butter, cheese, bacon, and eggs, milk, cream and flea, poultry and butchers' meat, ale, liquors and wine, candles, lamps and coal, linen, china, glass, furniture, homes and caul zges. But, sir, I must stop ; over a million a year goes to support a family to wham we mm supposed to be under some obligations over and share what we agreed to pay. What would this money do? It would build 6,076 houses at £l5O each, and would put an end to over-crowding. The sleeping beds -occupied by the dogs of her Majesty are in fire comport- ments, paved with asphalt and well supplied with water; n 3 over-crowding here. Each horse of her Majesty's stsd has two sets of clothing, ose for the day, and the other for night. Hot air is supplied to the carriage houses, In order to keep the royal carriages-well aired dining the cold ant/ Idamp weather. I think there are a few families Who will do whit of shouting during atm next few months who could make a few pointed remarks-about this matter. lot coarse would not presume to Compare a poor working-man with a royal dog, and merely quote history. In the following in- stance I quote tho " Despatch,7 August 25th, 1844 : Died, December 20th, 1840, one of, her MajestYs royal dogs, Dash, aged nine years, to the great grief of her Majesty. A bea-Atifol and expensive rnornament has bean erected over his last resting place, with the following inscription, written by her Majesty herself : Here lies Dashrthe hyourite spaniel of her Majesty Ctreen Victoria, by whose command this memorial was erected. He died on the 20th of December, 1840, in his 9th year. His attachment was without selitshness, his playfulness without malice, • his fidelity without deceit. Reader, it you would live beloved, and die regretted, profit by the example of Dash." So much for this phase of Royalty. Were it nor for its costly selfishness we might laugh at, it. Its ludicrous ele- rnente are enough to kill it, and would certainly achieve thie desirable end were it not for the army of hangers-on, to be found chiefly in the church, and ari9:meratical ciretes. .
I wilZ next week refer to Itoya:ty and the National ['eh% mother words the blessings of peace we have en- joyed during the past fifty years. CLIFFORD DIX.

lam not aiming at being a kill-joy, not in any sense, but I think a alight historical sketch of the past fity yeirs may not be out of place; of course not referring to the common people, they in this year of grace will have enough to de in the shouting line, and cannot be referred to now. Blackstone tells us that the sovereign is "pre-eminent," that in its political capacity it is "absolute perfection," and has, politically speaking, ,‘ absolute immortality." These are attributes, eir,generally given to another and a very different party who supposes himself a prisoner in Rome, and I might point in another direction, but I will refrain.

LAST NIGHTS PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. REFORMATION OF LAND Laws.—Lord CADOGAN pave notice that, on Thursday, he world call attention to recent legislation on land in Ireland, and introduce a bill.—The Loan CHANCELLOR gave notice to introduce a bill dealing with the transfer of land in England on the same day. TITHE BILL.—The Marquis of SALISBURY iutroduced a bill dealing with tithe c'targes, by which it was proposed to shift the incidence of that tax from the occupier to the owners of land.—The bill was read a first time. AGRICULTURAL DEERESSION.—EarI DR LAWARE moved that in the present depressed state of agriculture it was desirable to afford greater facilities for redemption of tithe rent charge in England and Wales.—The Marquis of SALIS- BURY, in reply, said reforms in the incidence of taxation were desirable, but agricultural distress could not be cured simply by legislation, and a return to Protection was not within the reasonable range of political politice—The motion was withdrawn, and the House adjourned. div.head: DISCUsSION ON THE IRISH QUESTION
div.p: DISCUsSION ON THE IRISH QUESTION
AT WIDNES.

The third of a series of meetings arranged by the Widnes.Division Liberal Association for the conside- ration of the Irish question' was held on Tuesday night in the Baths Assembly Room. There was a good attendance, and Mr. E. Carey presided. Mr. F. Cave opened the proceedings by reading a paper en. titled " The Irish evictions: Are they just ?" It waa through the land question, said Mr. C tve that most of the agitation, the strife, and the bloodshed had been caused in Ireland durieg the past few years. There were in the 151and120,000,000 acres, and this land was owned by a lomparatively few persons. Much ot it could not be sold at all en account of the law of entail, and that portion which it was possible to dispose of was so often bound up by eettremente, encombrances, qnit rentse and mortgages, that its sale Was a disealt matter. This' inability to pur- chase land even where they had the money, had been re- garded by the Irish as'a great grievance. 't be landlord was often so deeply in debt that he could not possibly make any improvements on tie estate, and' was compelled to ex- tort every penny he could get of rent from hie wretched tenants regardless of any real or fancied interests they had In their holdings. The rents were 'malty the highest in proportioi en the poorest and smallest holdings, and on these that had meet freqaently changed'owsers. M. Fin- lay Don referred to a landlord in 6bancgthee village, who was said to adoance his rent every second year, and who had one tenant paving £l6 for a holding rated at £2, and raised to its present value by the labours of the occupier. Other instances of the usjust manner in which rents are raised were given,. In some cases the least sign of improve- ment in the tenants' condition—a better horse, or coat, a new gate, a new piece of furniture, a bit at bacon banging up in the kitchen, had b ,n made the pretext, it Wee alleged, for raising rente.glMr. A. M. Sullivan, who spent a portion of his early life in one of the poorest parts of Iteland said "There can be no andet that the wretchedness of Irish pea- sant homem, their grievous disregard of comfort, neatness, or cleanliness, was derived almost entirely, from the Idea that improvements would invoke a rise of rent." It frequently happened a great while ago that a •man settled down on the edge of a bog, or by the side of a mountain, built a little cabin, and little by little drained' the bog or rep:lc-red the stones from the mountain side, fenced and farmed the land, and made sometimes a very poor, some- times productive farm. In most of these cases the tenant bad the consent, real or implied, of the landlord. Ia others the general Leling preealent in Ireland with reference to communal rights to waste land, and perhaps his own des- perate need, led the ',tient to assume that he might take nessession of the land. Whatever right he might have had to the land originally, ha or his descendants, who now oc- cupy it regard the little farm as peculiarly his own, for was knot his own labour, or that of his father, that created almost the entire value of the land. (Applause.) Recog- nising the man's right to enjoy the fruit of his labour, the landlord for a long period exacted but a low rent, but in proceseof time he concluded the land worth more and the rent wawraieed. Cases had been mentioned where the tenant was turned out of his holding a few years after he had made his improvemnts, withoutany compensation for them. Come mode of enforcing the payment of rent wa3 eviction, and although in England when a man was "turned out" little was thought of it, in Ireland it was regarded as a ter- rible outrage. The traditicne of the times when the land belonged to the people, the belief that the English 3till want to root out the Irish from the soil, the history of the penal laws, which tended to deprive the great mass of the people of every valuable right of citizenship, the harshness and emelt?' sometimes exercized by individual landlordq, the fact that the evicted tenant often had no occupation, no home for his family, and saw nothing before him but star- vation and the workhouse, had all combined to make the tanante.strongly resent and-resist every attempt totem any of them out of their heldicr, Mr. Cave dwe:,t upon the cruelty and injustice of many of the evictions, and drew a tartiblb picture of the miserable wretchedness they 'en- tailed. The reading of the paper was frequently interSup- tea with applause. An • interesting discussion followed.— Mr. Fairclongh made some remarks in favour of Home Rule, and advoca- ted the establishment of a Liberal Club in Widaes. Mr.?. Hartland observed that evictions were legal, but they were not just. He alluded to the enormous confine- tions—he called it robbery—of land by James the First, by. Cromwell, and by Wm. of Orange, and to the penal enact- ments interaled to crush and exterminate the Irish race. As Mr. Galion Duffy had saidamo man had dorm more to re- move the curse of Cromwell than Mr. Gladstone--(ap- planee)—but how cou!d Mr. Gladstone accomplish those great measures of reform needed for Ireland when he had to ' fight against the organised and tyrannical despotiona of an irresponsible House of Lords? (Applause.l It was the I opinion of Lord Cawper'S commission that owing to the failure of the crops and the reduction In the price of agricul- tural produce that the landlords of Irelalia were asking too mach of the peasantry i 3 the shape of routs—(hear, hear) and Sir General Redvera Buller had also impressed upon the landlords that they might reduce their rents. Under I these circarostances evicons were not only cruel but most an)ust. (Applause.) Mr. J. Fox said the English people had an almost religions devotion to contracts, but the contracts between the landlords and tenants of Ireland wera not free covenants but forced upon them, and theiefore not binding on the con- , science. ID the past Ireland had been reed by a system of landlordism introdaced by the British Government, and directed to the purpose of keeping the people poor and re- tarding the development of the resources of the country. If a tenant raised himself-so that he could wear a decent coat, and afford two good dinners a week, the lehdlord revaluad the land, and raised the rent up to such a point that the tenant would not have more than a bare subsistence for himself. This system was dying hard, but it was to be hoped that the wishea of England's greatest statesman Would prevail, and that at DO distant date Ireland would be ruled justly by her own people, under the supremacy of the same Sovereign as the English, Scotch, and Welshaand forming a union powerful and enduring becarase cemenied by affection. (Applause.) Mr. Quirke-also spoke. Mr. Showanalescrihed his enperiences on the Somerset- shire estate of the Duke of Cleveland, who allowed persons to reclaim and cultivate plots of land of from a quarter to half an acre on the uplands eta nominal rent oS Is tkl per year. INlen the land was made productive, his lordship did not rob the working man of his capital, which was his labour, but continued to raake the same nominal charge. This Was an example the Irish landloads ?Meat with bene- fit follow. (Applause.) His (Mr. Showan's) tote would go against avictioas. - . .

Mr. J. Morrison, in the course of a brief speech, said we were only just beginning to touch the fringe of the land qoeetion. The rental of l'reland was 14 millions a year, and of that—the "Times" was his authority—at lead 10 mil- lions went oat of the country to absentees. In his work on political economy, John Stuart Mill raid that a country that sent out more the.a it received would be a poor impov- erished country. and this draining of Ireland of its wealth could not go on for ever. tHear, bear.) From 1851 to 1885 the population. of Ireland had decreased from el mil- lions to under 5 in;ilions, and one would expect under these circumstanca th4t there would in less poverty, and that taxation would be lessened. The reverse was the result. In 1859 the total number receiving relief was 153,70 G, sad last year there were 705,000 persons in receipt of relief. In a good governed country it would be expected that the Government would have sympathy for tha people who had drifted into poverty of such a lamentable kind, and would try to reduce taxation, but in Ireland, as the population has decreased, and tbe poverty had become more keen, the taxa- tion had InCteased. ln 1851 Ireland contributed to tha

RUNCORN AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. A. meeting of the inhabitants of Runcorn, sum- monr d by Mr. P. Speakman, chairman of the Board of Commissioners, was held in Greenway-road Board I School, on Thursday night, under the presidency of that gentleman. There was a capital attendance, about 300 persons being present, including numerous tradesmen and working-men. The Revs. E. Maitland I Wood (vicar), W. Bryant, J. D. Thomas, and E. Williams; Messrs. W Mellor, F. J. Once, F. A. Lake, I J, Meadowcroft, and E. Marshall (secretary to the I Commiertioners), occupied seats on the platform. The Chairman having congratulated those present upon holding the meeting in a room which belonged to thereselves—(hear, hear,)—said they were met to , consider how to commemorate the Queen's Jubilee. I In different parts of the country different methods lead been resolved upon, and in some parts they had decided to do nothing at all. He did not want Run- corn to come under the latter category. He felt that the Runcorn people had a great amount of loyal de- votion to the Queen, and he hoped that they would have some lasting testimonial to the memory of our beloved Queen. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., who had been present, but was too unwell to stay, would fall in with anything they might do that night. He called upon the secretary to read a letter from the Rev. W. Preston, who wrote to the chairman that Runcorn ought to hand down to the unborn generations a suitable memento of the great event. So far as he was concerned he purposed erecting a Jubi- lee wall around Trinity Churchyard—(laughter) which he hoped would be a lasting rec3rd—" a thing of beauty and a joy foriever." If no generous hearted townsman blessed with a sound heart and a deep pocket does desire to be immortalised by building an accident hospital or erecting a something, then he trusted that "our wakeful, watchful, and useful Com- missioners would do what they can.' Mr. Pleston suggested as an alternative scheme the rebuilding of Waterloo Bridge, and its re-opening with im- posing ceremony, to include the town bell- ringer in uniform (laughter) and z.e- christened Victoria Bridge. A. further sugges- tion was the conversion of the common into a recrea- tion ground, and Mr. Preston offered to give up his freehold rights. The Chairman then alluded to communications he- bad received from the Prince of Wales with regard to the Imperial Institute, and remarked that it was for the inhabitants to decide whether they would contribute a donation to that proposed Institute or do something locally. Whatever 'was done musti be of an entirely voluntary character, and must be outside the rates altogether. A committee he had formed from the Board of Commissioners had met on several occaeione and discussed various schemes, but they had nothing definite to propose. One sug- gestion was that there should be a public holiday and that the venom) schools, churchee, and chapels should provide a tea party for their children, while a general fend should be- organised to give the aged poor and the waifs and strays that attended no school a good tea,. and ran present each child with a medal. The Vicar, in response to a call from the chair, made a speech, in which he said he admired Mr. Preston's determination, but the wall would no doubt , be a denominational wull—(laughter)—and they could I have nothing to do with it there. They must do , something, of which there could be no difference of 1 opinion and from which political feeling and sec- I tarian feeling were exeleaded. Looking round Ran- corn ates stranger, he had been more struck by the absence of anything in the shape of a hospital, except the one for infectious disease& behind the vicarage, and whieh appeared never to have been used at all. , He felt that Runcorn would accomplish a great deal I if by means of the wealthier classes, who, although they might not live in Runcorn, bad great interests in the town—the shareholders- and the managing direc- tors of their various works—they erected a building to contain half a dozen beds in which accident caeca might be treated. (Hear, hear.) The project to I erect an accident hospital wae one that would appeal to the sympathies of all claw& more than would any ! oter schetne. (Applause.) He was also in favoure of a procession of friendly soeietiee, and if they would ' allow him to-suggest, without wishing to be thought in any way a denominationalist, or to tread on any- , ones corns, that the Perish Church should be used ' for the purpose of gieing some public expression of ' thanks to the Almighty for the great benefits they had received underthe peaceful rule of their Sovereign. (A.pplitere.) The Chairman said'ke had inet received a commu- nication to the effect that the CheehireFootball Union wouldiee glad-to contribute a donation of ilo towards a cottage hospital. (A.pplianse.a He (the chairman). would be glad to give s-donation of IS towards the- same object. The itev. E. Veit i itll4, while heartily supporting the sug- gestion for the erection of- an accident hospital, spoke strongly in favour of the provision of a recreation ground. (Applause). The Rev. J. Di Thomas argued in favour of establishing , a scholarship at Liverpool Uhiversit7 College, which should, I be competed for by-the beys in their public schools. (Ap-- plause). Mr. Once seworted the- proposal to establish a cottage hospital, and said that he would be glad to subscribe Vir (Hear, beam) An idea which found favour with the Corn- missimets was that there should be a treat to all the poor children and poor people in-the town, so that every person. might share Is the rejoicings Do MacDougall , said the suggestion of a cottage hospital+ was 14 very excellent one, but the first consideration was the wherewithal. Alluding to the recreation ground, Dr. Mac- Dougall said that in Runcorn Hill they 13;c1 a recreation ground which was free to all and where the air was as pure as could be foond in any. part of Cheshire. He strongly supaorted the proposal to establish a scholarship, while-he also suggested thatnome measures be taken by the granting of subscriptions to enable patients suffering from rheuma- tism and. consumption to Pe sent to such instieutiona as. might be found at Buxton and at Southport. He moved, however, that a committee representative of all classes alemeldbe formed for the consideration of the various ways in which the Queen's Jubilee might be celebrated. Mr. W. :law seconded, the proposal, and suggested that if a proceseion took place it should be headed by a petition , in favour of closing public-houses en the Sundays. (Laugh- ter.) . Mr. H. Jahnsoo mentioned, the question of public baths, upon which he said many ratepayers would like to have eorne information. The Chairmanreplied that the question of baths was one /or the ratepayeas only., and he thought that anything that was done by that meeting should be something of evvoitin- tars, character which could, not be paid for out of the pub- lic funds. I Mr. Bellamy said 'that the Commissioners could &did either an accidenthospital cr baths out of the rates and if a resokition WAS passed-by that meeting the Commissioners would be made aware of what the pebple really, required. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Lake seconded the propowal for a cottage hospital, observing that he did, not know of any movement which would be more generously or more widely scpnorbed. He thought that a sueficient income would be raised by means of mllectims at the various churches arta:chapels and by subscriptions from the works. He did not think they eboald pcl any scheme on the rates, as it would compel all people in the town to contribute whetter they wished or not. (A.pplause.) Mr. Bolt suggested that the question 3:1 an accident hos- pital should be deferred for future consideration, as it was one which the friendly societies did, not regard with , favour. , Mr. W. Littler, who said he represented one of the largest friendly sotieties in the town, said that the members of the , friendly societies had not yet considered any proposal, but after that meeting they would be ready to take any quee- Men into consideration, and give the most feasible practical . help. To his mind the most popular proposal was the erection of baths. Mr. James Whinyates said that the Commissioners had been conshlering the baths question fox seven years,. and they were told that evening that it was still under con- sideratiore. (Laughter.) He heartily supported the pro- posal to erect baths. Mr. Se. Coventry alto spoke in favour of baths. Mr. Jones (a working-man) protested against any money being taken out of the pockets of the ratepayers, 1 who were already pressed beyond their means. (Applause.) I If he understood the principle of the Jubilee, it was that tha rich should bless the poor, and they would not do that by taking money out of the poor man's pocket. (Cheers.) i Mr George Littler suggested that a scheme should be corn- minced for freeing Runcorn Bridge. Mr Meadowcroft, alluding to the questica of public baths, , said that they could not be made self-supporting, ad he • suggested that those who seemed to have such confidence in them should form a limited company and take shares. . I A protracted discussion took place upon the various , schemes suggested, the propose' to erect bathe evidently meeting with most favour amongst the audience. Ulti.

LOCAL,TOWNSHIP MEETINGS.
RUNCORN.

The annual meeting of the ratepavers of Runcorn for the purpose of electing overseers ani transacting other business, was held in Bethesda. Schoolroom on Thursday evening. Mr. W. Handley was Noted to the chair. On the motion of M. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. Firth, Messrs. C. Cooke and W. Brookes were appointed to audit the ac- 'counts of the :luncorn Burial Board, and it was resolved that their report should be received en the 21st April.— With regard ta the appointment of overseers. the Cuairman pointed out that Mr. Whittal;er and himself had been in office continuously for ten years, and he considered that it Iwould be a wise course, and only fair to other gentlemen, ito make a change.—Mr. Coleburn said it would be a pity to lose the services of two gentlemen who did their work so i well, and Mr.. Firth expressed the hope that the magis- trates would.again select them—lt was then resolved that the followiag list should be•sabinitted to the justices : Messrs. W. Biandley, W. Whittaker, Edwin Imison, Samuel Taylor, W. H. Rogerson, William Mellor, and William Han- kinson.—Tice Chairman submitted the accounts for tho year, which showed that OEI March 26Lh, 1886, there was a. balance in hand in favour of the township of £530 5s 3d. and there had been realised from the Met rate of 10d in the A, the SUM Of £2,070 Ss 4d, and from the second rate of in in the 2/Me sum of £2,507:0s Id. Sundry items brought up the total receipts for the year to £5,113. The overseers bad paid to the Guardians first half year 21,456, second half yemr £1,313 ; to the School Board, first half year £650, second half year £.500; and to the Burial Board had been paid 2220. Salary and office expenses anasunted to -2220 19s sd. There was at the end of the year a balance of £66624 al in favour of the township.—The Chairman read a letter from the agent to Colonel Gamble, of St. Helens, asking for an additional 25 per cent to be allowed him on the rates of his property, under section 3of the Poor Rate Collection Act, 21:O.-The Chairmanexplained that the corn- pending clauses of the Act were not in force in Runcorn, and after some discussion it was unanimously resolved that the vestry saw no reason to depart from the custom hitherto pursued.—A vote of thanks ta the Chairman con- cluded the proceedings._

It is too early to speak with confidence on agricultural prospects, but undoubtedly the weather, up to the beginning of this week, was most favourable as a preparation for seed time. That there will be no lack of mone- tary support for any forward movement in trade is abundantly proved by the great events in the money market which have stirred the last three or four months. The subscriptions to the successive booms of Guinness, Allsopp, and Hotchkiss of course do not represent actual cash in pocket. A modest friend of mine told me that he had applied for nothing less than £20,000 of the Allsopp stock. As this involved lodgment of a cheque for £l,OOO, and as literary men as a rule do not always keep so . large a balance at their bank, the announcement iwas calculated to raise this bold speculator in the estimation of his friend. It turned out, however, that the transaction was one that did not neces- sarily involve the possession of more than a five pound note. His bankers managed the whole business, sent in the cheque, receiving the exceed- ingly modest allotment, immediately sold it, de- ducted the charges and interest on the £l,OOO, and handed the balance to the resolute speculator.
